blocks.h: A CENTIMETRE A MONTH
Roya Publication No. 104
by Chew Z
SYNOPSIS

A hair salon in southern Tehran has its street window painted over, because that is the law. Inside, every woman takes her scarf off. Outside, every woman puts it back on. It is the same women and the same four metres of ground, and the difference is a door.

A girl of fourteen comes to work at the back, washing hair. Her aunt gives her an old exercise book and tells her to write down what is there — how long it was, what was in it. The girl asks who wants it. Nobody wants it, her aunt says. Write it down anyway.
She is told she must cover her own hair so that men are not stirred. She cannot make the reason work, and for five years nobody will help her make it work.

And when her hands are in the water she begins to know, without wanting to and without being able to stop, what each head has already cost the woman wearing it. A morning. An afternoon in a van. Four years of six o'clock telephone calls. A room with no window. Two messages, one of them to somebody's father.
So the book in the drawer grows a second column, in smaller and smaller handwriting, and by the time she is nineteen it is the only place on earth where any of it has been added up.
Then a man comes to the shop with a folder, and he is polite, and he wants to know who started it.
A NOTE FROM THE AUTHOR
This book has no names in it. That is the point of it, and it is also the reason this note is longer than the ones at the front of the other books in this series.

Nothing in the story happened. The shop is invented, the girl is invented, her aunt is invented, and so are all five of the women whose accounts the book turns on. What she can do with her hands cannot be done.
What it cost them is not invented. Every price in that book is an ordinary price, of an ordinary kind, paid in that country by an enormous number of women whose names are written down nowhere.
But some names are written down, and this is where they go.
THE WOMEN THE BOOK COULD NOT NAME

On the sixth of Dey 1396 — the twenty-seventh of December 2017 — Vida Movahed stood on a utility box on Enghelab Street in Tehran, took off her white headscarf, tied it to a stick and held it up. She was thirty-one. She said nothing at all. She was arrested the same day. She had a nineteen-month-old daughter.

Over the following weeks other women did the same thing, alone, in Tehran and in other cities. Police reported twenty-nine arrests inside about a month. Azam Jangravi was one of the women who climbed up; she was dismissed from her job and later left the country.

And then the municipality welded inverted-V metal caps onto the tops of the utility boxes, so that the tops were no longer flat, so that nobody could stand on one. That is in this book because I have never been able to stop thinking about it. Somebody drew it. Somebody ordered the metal. Somebody was paid for a day's driving.

In Tir 1397 — July 2018 — Maedeh Hojabri, a teenager, was detained over videos of herself dancing that she had posted on Instagram, and was shown on state television saying she was sorry. Women across the country answered by posting videos of themselves dancing. Nobody organised that and there is no first name attached to it.

In Shahrivar 1398 — August 2019 — Saba Kord Afshari was sentenced to twenty-four years, fifteen of them for taking off her headscarf in public, the charge framed as spreading corruption and prostitution. She was twenty years old. The sentence was later reduced and she has since been released.

On the twenty-fifth of Shahrivar 1401 — the sixteenth of September 2022 — Mahsa Jina Amini, twenty-two years old, died in the custody of the guidance patrol in Tehran. What followed is not in this book, because this book stops a few weeks later, which is the point at which the girl telling it still knows nothing.

Not one of these women appears in the story. The series has a rule against it and I have never broken it. The narrator refuses to write Jina Amini's name for her own reasons, in her own entry, and those reasons are hers and not mine.
WHAT WOMEN HAVE SAID ABOUT IT THEMSELVES
I did not invent the feeling of the thing, and I want to be exact about where it came from.

Iran International interviewed Iranian women about the first time they went out in public with their heads uncovered. They described wind in their hair and cool air on the face and the neck, felt in public for the first time — in some cases at forty years old, in one case at sixty. One woman described crying while driving in a T-shirt, feeling air on her skin. A woman of forty said she wished she had felt it at twenty rather than at forty. A woman of seventy had stopped covering at sixty; another said it made her feel like a teenager again. The words they used were freedom, relief, lightness, power.
And beside that, the fear. Scarves carried in bags in case. Looking around constantly while walking. One woman's heart racing for the whole of a first outing.

One of them said something that is the engine of this entire book: that seeing other women without headscarves gradually reduced her anxiety — that watching others make the same choice gave her more confidence.

She was made braver by strangers she never met and never thanked, and by walking past the next woman she made her braver in turn. That is what this book is about, and no part of it required anybody to organise anything.

Human Rights Watch published an interview by Tara Sepehri Far with a fifty-one-year-old woman given the pseudonym Pendar, who with two friends decided to walk crowded main streets uncovered on Wednesdays and Saturdays:

"We realized that hijab is the identity of Islamic Republic, so to speak. And we decided together that we will stop wearing it." > > "It was very scary and difficult for us at the beginning, but we decided to do it anyways and accepted all its consequences." > > "Schoolchildren would pass in their bus clapping and waving their hands for us. Now we get less of those." > > "There are still people who look at us in disgust."

Three friends deciding over tea is the largest unit of organisation anyone has documented in the whole of this change. I want that stated plainly, because it is the hardest fact in the file to believe and the most important one in the book.
Fatemeh Jamalpour, an Iranian journalist living in exile, said this on WBUR's On Point:
"This young generation made us a braver and better version of ourselves."

That sentence is why the girl telling this story is fourteen and the woman who teaches her is fifty-four. The usual direction of courage is reversed, and it is reversed in the record, not in my imagination.
WHERE THE BOOK'S FACTS COME FROM
The four interludes are the book's history and I am not going to tell it twice. What follows is where each of them comes from, so that a reader who wants to go and check can.

The first interlude — the oldest hair law, and the fact that it specified which women must cover and forbade the slave and the prostitute to, on pain of hot pitch — is the Middle Assyrian laws, roughly thirty-four centuries old. The old woman telling it does not know she is quoting a statute.

The second — that the two Qur'anic passages on covering do not contain the word for hair, and that hair was classified as 'awrah later by juristic argument resting partly on a report whose chain of transmission has been disputed from inside the tradition — is a live argument and not a settled question. Sisters in Islam put the plain version publicly in 2015 and a mufti answered it within the week. Both positions are still standing. The book states that it is an argument and takes no side, and neither do I.

The third — Greek and Roman practice, the Mishnah, the letter about the angels, and the evidence that the preaching did not describe the street — rests on Grace Stafford's study of late antiquity, in which only about a quarter of some hundred and fifty surviving female portrait sculptures show a covered head, and in which the mosaics show the mistress covered and the attendant beside her bare.

The fourth — the map of where covering is law today — is Iran's Article 638; Afghanistan's decree of Ordibehesht 1401 and the virtue law of Sanbula 1403, whose Article 13 is quoted as the man quotes it; Aceh's provincial statute; and Sudan, 1989 to 2019.
WHAT THE BOOK DOES NOT SAY, AND I WILL

The forty years. Compulsory covering in Iran was not legislated at once. In 1357 it was presented as a recommendation and the protests of the eighth of March were answered by saying so. It was required in government offices within about a year and law by 1362. There was no day on which anybody announced that the recommendation had become an order. Then 1393. 1396, the utility boxes, the welded caps. 1397. 1398. Then Shahrivar 1401, and the guidance patrol's street function effectively ending that winter — after which, in Ordibehesht 1402, the judiciary drafted a Hijab and Chastity bill because the patrol had stopped. A parliamentary committee expanded it from fifteen articles to seventy-four. It passed. And in Aban 1403 the Supreme National Security Council suspended it, and it has never been brought into force. Nothing was repealed. The rule is still there.

Where the enforcement went. Not away — sideways. At least fifty business premises sealed across eight cities in 1404, with more in Borujerd and Kashan than in Tehran. Undercover officers announced for cafés and concerts. IMSI-catchers, contactless national-identity card readers and city cameras checked against government databases in Isfahan province, producing tens of thousands of warning messages — sent to the woman and to her relatives. That last clause is the whole of the fourth account in this book.

The figure everybody quotes. Women appearing without a headscarf after the 1401 uprising rose by 24 per cent — from Avenia Ghazarian's working paper Veils of Change, cited by Mohammad Ali Kadivar in MERIP in Khordad 1405. It measures appearances tracked on social media. It is not a street count and not a survey. I would rather say that than repeat a number without saying what it is.

And the hair. Hair grows at a rate conventionally taken as about a centimetre a month, and what the body is doing is laid down in the shaft as it grows, which is why hair is used in research as a backwards-readable record of chronic stress over roughly the previous six months. And after a severe shock the follicles do not release the hair at once: they rest, and shedding begins two to three months later.
Which means the hair does not come out during the crisis.
It comes out afterwards, when the thing is over and everybody has stopped asking.

That is the only reason the third account in this book exists. A woman's hair came out in the week her sister came home. The body bills late, and it very often bills the woman who was not arrested. The book never names any of this, because the girl telling it has no vocabulary for it and should not have.
WHAT I AM ARGUING, AND WHAT I AM NOT

The argument in this book — that fear worked like a currency and that the state debased it by spending it, one woman at a time, for forty years — is mine. It is not a finding. No researcher told me that. I think the book earns it, and you are entitled to disagree.

And I want to be straight about the opposite: no source I could find says that the patrols stopped because they were overwhelmed by numbers. Analysts read the easing as political calculation, including the calculation of not opening a second front during a war. The government has never explained itself. It is not explained in this book either.

What I will stand behind is the shape of it. Nothing was repealed. No retreat was announced. The rule is where it was, word for word, and the only thing between that street and the old price is that nobody has decided to start collecting again.
A thing nobody admits giving can be taken back without anybody admitting that either.
And the last thing, which is the reason I wrote it.

There was no leader. There was no plan, no committee, no first woman, no name for the man with the folder to write down. And that is not the gentle version of this story. It is the hard one. A movement with a leadership distributes its costs, keeps a roll of its dead, and can at least tell a woman that what happened to her was part of something.
This had none of that. Every one of them paid the whole price by herself, for herself, and almost all of them were thanked by nobody, and there is no building anywhere whose job it is to add it up.
That is what the second column is for.

I. THE WINDOW
Khanom Ansari told me this in my first week, with her head over the basin and her eyes shut, because I had asked her a question and she was the only person who answered it instead of laughing.
She said: you think this started with us.

She said her own mother had told her that in the oldest places, long before anybody here prayed the way we pray, there was a law about hair. Not a law telling women to cover. A law telling them which women had to and which were forbidden.
A wife covered. A widow covered. They went out into the main road with their heads covered and everyone could see what they were.

And a woman who was owned, and a woman who sold herself, were not allowed to. Their heads had to be bare. That was the law. If one of them put something over her head and was caught, they poured hot pitch on her and beat her fifty times. And the man who saw her do it and said nothing to anybody, they beat him fifty times too, and put a hole through his ears so that people would know what he was.
I said, so the covering was to protect them.
She had soap on her forehead. I wiped it off with my thumb.

She said: child, think about what you just said. If it was to keep women safe from men, who would you cover first? The one with nobody. The one who is out at night. The one anybody can do anything to.
She said: they did not cover her. They forbade her. On pain of burning.
She said: so it was not a wall. It was a label. It was so that a man in the road could tell, without asking, whose you were.
Then she said the water was going cold, and I turned the tap, and she did not say anything else about it for four years.
TO THE SHOULDER. A CLIP SHE HAD FORGOTTEN.
The first thing I learned in the shop was the window.

It is a big window onto the street and it has been painted over on the inside, cream, two coats, and over the paint there is a curtain that does not open. This is because the law says no man walking past may see a woman in here with her head uncovered.
We painted the window. Nobody painted the men.

My aunt put her hand flat on it the first morning and said, this is the law, and if a man out there can see in, they can shut me. I said who can. She said somebody can, and that is enough to know, which I have since learned is the single most accurate sentence anybody has ever said to me about this country.

On the wall behind the till there is a frame with a paper in it and a number on the paper, and the number is the licence. She renews it every year. She says if the number stops, the chairs are just chairs.
I have thought about that for five years and I have still not worked out which part of this is the religion and which part is the municipality.

I was fourteen. It was Dey and the pavements were wet. I had come to live with my aunt in the autumn because my mother had gone onto nights at the plant and could not do both ends of my school day. That is the reason I was given and I believed it for five years, which tells you something about me that will come up again.
Six chairs along the mirrors. Two dryers, one of which works. A tin of boiled sweets for children nobody brings.
My job was the basin.

There are two of them at the back under the hot pipe, with a dip in the porcelain where a neck goes. You learn the temperature first, and you test it on the inside of your wrist and not on your fingers, because fingers lie. Too hot and a woman says nothing and never comes back; too cold and she tells you at once, which is better. I got a head down to nine minutes inside a month and I would like that noticed, because nobody noticed it at the time.

Towel across the shoulders before the water, not after. Thumb above the ear so it goes back and not down. Ask twice — once at the start and once in the middle — and the second one is the one that counts, because the first one is manners.
And every woman who comes through that door takes her scarf off.

It took me years to notice that this was strange. Out on the pavement every head is covered. Inside, past the paint, every head is bare. Same women. Same four metres of ground. The entire difference is a door, a tin of cream paint, and a number in a frame.

There were six in by noon that first day and I washed four. My aunt cut three and did a colour and talked the whole time without stopping once — a wedding in Karaj, a cousin's car, the price of chicken — and the radio was on above the mirrors the way it is always on, a man reading something about the currency in the voice they keep for that.

The last one before lunch had a clip in her hair she had forgotten about, a little gold one with a bird on it. It came out in my hand under the water and she laughed and said her daughter had put it there in the morning and she had been walking round the whole district with a bird on her head and not one person had told her.

I have thought about that woman more than she would believe. She walked past the fruit shop and the pharmacy and the bakery with a bird on her head, in a country where what is on a woman's head is a matter for the government, and the government did not notice the bird.
When she had gone my aunt gave me a school exercise book with a cardboard cover. Not new. It had somebody's sums in the front, which she tore out.
She said: write down what's there.
I said what do you mean, what's there.
She said: the hair. How long it was. Anything in it.
I said for what. Does somebody want it.
And she said no. Nobody wants it. Write it down anyway.

So I wrote to the shoulder, a clip she had forgotten, and I put the book in the drawer under the till next to the appointment book, and I did not think about it again for a week, and that is the first line of a document that a man from the government took away from me five years later, because he wanted a name and it has none in it.
DOWN HER BACK, AND NOT ONE GREY HAIR AT FIFTY-SIX.
I am not going to use many names in this.

Partly that is the book's fault — there are no names in it, not one, in five years, in nearly four hundred entries, and after that long you stop reaching for them. And partly it is that a shop does not work by names. A shop works by slots. The woman who comes every second Thursday. The first Saturday of the month. The one who always wants it done before a Friday and always says she does not mind waiting and always minds.
So that is how they will come, and I am not going to pretend it is modesty.

My aunt does not get a name either. She is Khaleh. That is a word for your mother's sister and it is the only thing I have ever called her, including once in an office, in front of a man, when a name would have been more use. And the man who came for the book at the end of all this does not get one, because he is the only person in this account who had the power to write mine down, and I have decided he can go without.
That winter it was the money.

I did not understand the money. What I understood was bread, because I bought the bread — that the number on the note in my pocket stayed where it was and the loaf got smaller, and that nobody had announced it, and that there was no day on which it had happened.
What they argued about was whose fault it was.

The woman who comes every second Thursday said it was the Americans. She said it the way you say a thing you have read your whole life. I would like to record that the Americans have been in that shop every second Thursday for five years and have never once had their hair done.

Khanom Ansari, who came on the first Saturday, said it was ours, meaning the government's, and said it flatly, the way old people say a thing they have said many times and have given up expecting to be contradicted.

Somebody said it was the last lot. Somebody else said it was the lot before them. One woman — she only came twice, I never found out what she was called — said can everybody please be quiet for one minute, I want to hear the end of this.
Nobody won.

Nothing in that room ever finished. Somebody would say the sentence that ought to have ended it, and then a dryer would go on, and twenty minutes later it would start again from the beginning in a different mouth with the same opinion. In five years I never once saw a woman in that shop change her mind about anything except a colour.

And here is the part that took me longer. We were not arguing with anybody. There was nobody in the room to argue with. The government was never in that shop. It was on the radio, and it was in the frame on the wall, and it was in the paint on the window, and it never once had to come in and sit down and answer a question.
I said that to my aunt on the walk home. I said which one of them is right.
She said about the money?
I said about any of it.
She said: Baran, in this country you can be right for forty years and it makes no difference to one single thing. Then she said we needed eggs.
That was also the month I asked my question for the first time, at the basin, with my hands in somebody's hair.
I said: why do I have to cover my hair.
She said: because that is the rule.
I said: I know it's the rule. Why is it the rule.
And she said: so that men don't get ideas.
So I thought about that properly, because I am a literal person and it was offered as a reason.

I am in charge of the contents of a stranger's head. Not my head. His. There is a man somewhere in this city I have never met and never will, and his thoughts are my department. I have held the post since I was nine. Nobody interviewed me. There is no training, the hours are every hour I am outside the house, there is no overtime, and the only performance review is conducted in the street by whoever feels like it.
And if he has the thought anyway it is still my fault, because the job has no upper limit and no definition of success.
I said: then it is the men.
She did not hear me, or she heard me and let it go, which with her is the same thing.

The woman in the chair had hair all the way down her back and was fifty-six years old and did not have one grey hair in it, not one, and I wrote that down because it was the most interesting thing that happened to me that day.
CUT TO THE JAW THAT MORNING, BY HERSELF, BADLY.

In Bahman a woman stood on top of one of the grey metal boxes on a pavement in the middle of town, the kind with cables in it, and took her scarf off and tied it to a stick and held it up over her head.
She did not shout anything. That was the part the shop could not get past. She did not say one word. She stood up there and held it up and let people look.
They took her away the same day.
Then over the next weeks other women did it. Here and in two other cities. On boxes, on a bollard, on a wall. Each one alone. Each one quiet. Each one taken away.
And then they welded the caps on.
Somebody went out with a van and a welder and put a metal peak on the top of every one of those boxes in the district, a little roof, so the top is not flat any more. So there is nowhere to stand.
I walked past them for years and never got used to it, and I want to set out what I admire about it, because I do admire it.
They did not take the boxes away, or put a camera on them, or post a man. They changed the shape of the top of the box so that a woman cannot stand on it.

Somebody drew that. Somebody sat down with a pencil and worked out the angle. Somebody costed the metal and somebody signed off the costing and somebody was paid for a week's driving. Somewhere in this city there is a man who had a week where his job was boxes, and I think about him more often than I think about several of my relatives, and what I want to know is what he said at dinner.
Because you cannot say nothing. You come home and somebody asks what you did today.
And it worked. That is the other thing. Nobody has stood on one since.

So the first lesson this country ever taught me about itself was not about women and it was not about God. It was that if you make the top of the box pointy, the problem goes away, and nobody has to have an argument with anybody.
That was also the week my aunt burned the books.
She did it on a Thursday night in the yard, in the half-barrel the man downstairs uses for rubbish, in her indoor slippers, and I came down because I could smell it from the window.

Eighteen years of appointment books. The fat kind with the ring binding, one a year, and every page of every one of them is names. Names and dates and times. Who sat in that chair, on which afternoon, at what hour.
I said Khaleh, what are you doing.
She said go up.
I said those are the books.
She said I know what they are. Go up.

I stood on the step and watched her feed them in one at a time and push them down with a stick when they went slack, and she did not cry and she did not hurry, and when it was done she washed her hands at the tap in the yard for a long time.

In the morning there was a brand new appointment book in the drawer with nothing in it, and my exercise book beside it, and she pushed the exercise book towards me with two fingers and said, you keep that one.
I did not ask her why for five years.

That was not restraint. I was fourteen, and the adults around me did things, and some of them were strange, and you did not interrogate it any more than you interrogated the weather. My aunt burning eighteen years of her own paperwork in a barrel went into the same part of my head as my mother's shifts and the water going off on Tuesdays.
She came in at noon that day with her hair cut to the jaw. She had done it herself in the night with the kitchen scissors, badly, and she would not let anybody fix it.
I wrote that down. Cut to the jaw that morning, by herself, badly.
I thought she was upset about the news.
TO THE WAIST. CAME IN BRAIDED AND WOULD NOT LET ME UNDO IT.

Esfand is the worst month and the best month, because everybody wants to be new for the year. We did fourteen heads one Wednesday and I did not sit down between eight in the morning and nine at night, and my aunt gave me more money at the end of it than I had ever held, and I spent it on a scarf for my mother, which I am aware of.
There are two books in the drawer under the till and I should set out what the other one is, because later it matters.

Here is what the appointment book is. A woman telephones or leans in the door, and you write her name and the day and the time and what she wants. That is all. Every shop in the country has one. The bakery has one. It is the most ordinary object in any business anywhere.
And here is the other thing it is, which I did not see for years.
It is a list of every woman in this district who has sat in that room with nothing on her head, and the date she did it, and the hour.

Nobody keeps it for that. Nobody looks at it that way. It is appointments. But if a person ever wanted such a list, there would be no need to go and build one, because the law already requires a woman like my aunt to keep it, in a drawer, in a shop with a painted window, and to be able to produce it when asked.

I want to be fair here, because I have had five years to work out who to blame for that and the answer is nobody. Nobody designed it. It is just what happens when you make a room where the rule is suspended and then put a number on the wall. You cannot have the exception without the paperwork. The paperwork is the price of the exception.
In Esfand I started filling the exercise book in properly, every head, not only the interesting ones. It took about forty seconds. I did it standing at the till while the dryer ran.

To the shoulder. To the waist. Short at the back and long at the front, which was the thing that year. Grey underneath and black on top. Thin at the crown, and she knows, and does not want it mentioned.

A woman came in on the last Thursday with her hair in one plait to her waist and would not let me undo it to wash. Her mother had plaited it that morning and her mother was not well and she wanted to keep it until Friday. So I washed around it, which cannot actually be done, and we both pretended it had worked, which is the most Iranian forty minutes of my life.
I wrote her down. One line. To the waist, came in braided and would not let me undo it.

There was nothing else to write. There was no second line yet. For the first part of that book there is only ever one line, and when I look at those pages now, the white space under each of them is the loudest thing on the paper.
TO THE SHOULDER, AND THE SAME PARTING SHE HAS HAD ALL HER LIFE.
Khanom Ansari came at ten on the first Saturday of every month and had done since before I was born.

She was about seventy. She wore grey. She carried a cloth bag with a zip and had the exact money folded in her hand before she sat down, which my aunt said she had done for twenty years, and which my aunt said was a thing people of that generation do so as never to owe anybody anything for even one minute.
Her hair came to her shoulder. Thin, very clean, set rather than cut, and the parting on the left.

That parting is in my book more times than anything else in it, because she came every month for four and a half years and it never moved. Not a centimetre. I used to wet it and comb it and watch it fall back into the same line as though the line had been cut into her scalp.
I thought it was just how old ladies are.

She was the only person who ever answered my question. Everybody else either laughed, or said because that is the rule, or said because men are animals — which is offered as a defence of the men, and I would like somebody to sit down and look at that sentence properly one day — or said you will understand when you are older, which is what people say when they do not know and have decided that time will cover for them.

Khanom Ansari asked me what I had actually meant by it. That is all she did. And when I had explained it badly for about a minute she shut her eyes and told me the thing about the old law, the one about which women had to cover and which were forbidden, and the hot pitch, and the man with the hole through his ears.
And then she said the thing I did not understand for three years. She said: it was not a wall, child. It was a label.

I wrote down to the shoulder, and the same parting she has had all her life, which I now think is the most informative line in the entire book, and which I wrote because I had nothing else to say about her.

I liked her and I want that in here, because the way I have described her so far makes her sound like a wise old woman out of a story and she was nothing of the kind. She was a ferocious gossip. She had views on a serial she watched with the sound off at our place and narrated herself, including the parts she had invented. She once told a woman in the next chair, to her face, with no preamble, that her son was a waste of a good education. She called my aunt's coffee an insult and she said it every month for four and a half years and my aunt kept making it the same way, and I have never decided which of them was winning.
She did not talk about herself. In four and a half years, not once, not one fact.
It was the hottest week of the following summer before I knew a single thing about her life, and I did not get it out of her mouth.
THIN AT THE LEFT TEMPLE, AND IT HAS NOT CAUGHT UP.
This is the entry where the book changes and I want to put down exactly what happened, in order, because for a long time I thought I had made it up.
It was the middle of Farvardin. The year was new. The shop was quiet in the way it goes quiet after Nowruz, when everybody has already had their hair done and nobody has any money left.
A woman came in at about four in the afternoon who had not been in before. Forties. A green coat. She stood just inside the door for longer than people stand there.

My aunt did her consultation at the chair, which is the normal thing — you sit them down, you talk about what they want, you lift the hair at the sides. And then she walked her back to the basin and handed her to me, and said, Baran will take care of you, in the voice she uses for people who are nervous, which is a different voice from her ordinary one.
The woman sat down. I put the towel across her shoulders. I asked her to lean back.
And she did not lean back.

She sat forward with her hands in her lap and she looked at the taps. I waited. My aunt was at the mirrors with her back to us doing somebody's roots and I could see in the glass that she was watching.
After a while the woman said, I do this myself, normally.
I said, that's all right.
She said, I have done it myself for a long time.
I said, you can keep your head up if you like, some people prefer it, I can do it with a jug.
And she thought about that and then she said no, it's fine, and she leaned back, and she put her neck into the dip in the porcelain, and I turned the water on and put my hand in her hair.
And I knew.
I am going to try to say this properly and it is going to sound mad, and I have no interest in persuading anybody.

It was not a picture. Nothing went dark and nothing flashed and there was no voice. It was more like the way you know your own telephone number — you do not look it up, you do not work it out, you do not remember it; it is simply there, and if somebody asks you for it, it comes out of your mouth.

What was there was this. That she had been put into a van, once, a long time ago. That they had taken hold of her hair to get her into it. And that she had not let another human being touch the back of her head since the week it happened.
That was all. No van in my head, no scene — three facts sitting in me the way the number sits in you, with no edges and nothing attached, and I had not had them two seconds earlier.

My hands kept going. That is the part I think about. My hands did not stop. I rinsed her and I asked is it still good and she said yes, and I did the second wash, and I did the ends, and I wrapped her and walked her up to the chair, and I said nothing at all.
And then I went and stood by the back door with the yard in front of me and shook.

I told myself I had made it up. Out of the way she sat, and the green coat, and the shop going flat about the boxes, and being fourteen and reading too much into things. I was extremely reasonable about it for three weeks. I have since noticed that I am at my most reasonable when I have decided in advance what the answer is going to be, which is a thing I learned off the radio.
I did not write the second line that day. The page for the fifteenth of Farvardin has one line on it, thin at the left temple, and nothing under it.
I wrote the second line in Mordad, four months later, when I knew. You can see it. The ink is different and the hand is worse, because by then my hand was worse.
SHORT, AND GOING WHITE AT THE FRONT ONLY.
It happened again in Ordibehesht and then it happened again eight days later and after that I stopped being able to call it nothing.
So I tested it, which I am not proud of.

There was the woman who came every second Thursday, the one who thought it was the Americans. I knew a certain amount about her from the room, the way you do — a husband, two sons, a sister in Mashhad, a knee that needed doing. So I washed her and I waited to see whether what came was anything I could have got from the chairs.

Nothing came. Nothing at all. I had my hands in her hair for seven minutes and there was no number and no fact, and I stood there feeling faintly insulted, as though she were holding something back out of meanness. Then I understood, and I had to put the water on cold and hold my wrists under it.

Nothing came because there was nothing. She had never been stopped. Not once, not in fifty-nine years, not even leaned out of a car at. She had got all the way through her whole life inside the rule and the rule had never once put its hand on her, and she did not know that this was a remarkable thing to be able to say, because why would she. Nobody compares.
I wrote nothing on the second line and I looked at it for a while.

My aunt saw me looking at it. She did not ask what I was writing. In five years she never once asked me what was on the second line, and she never once looked, and I know she never looked because the book stayed exactly where I left it, and I am the sort of person who notices a book that has been moved.
She did say one thing, that spring, out of nowhere, with her back to me.
She said, you do not have to put everything in there.
And I said, I know.
And she said, I am saying you do not have to. Then she went and dealt with somebody's foils.

I have turned that over for years. I think she was telling me I was allowed to stop. I think she was also telling me she knew what I had started. Both of those can be true of her at the same time; that is what she is like.
In Khordad the heat arrived and the question came back, and this time it came back with teeth.

Because here is Tir and Mordad in this city. Forty degrees and more. The shop is a closed room with two dryers and a hot pipe along the back wall. I worked in there in a long tunic with sleeves to the wrist and a scarf pinned at the throat, and I walked home in it, and I stood at the bus stop in it with the pavement going soft under me.
And the reason — the entire reason, the whole and only reason — is so that a man I have never met does not have a thought.

I have costed this. In Tir I am wearing about four hundred grams of cloth I do not need, in a room at forty-four degrees, for nine hours a day, six days a week, and the fan has not worked since the Wednesday before. And the entire return on that, the whole of what the country gets for it, is the uninterrupted inner life of a man on a bus.
I would like it recorded that the fan is the part I find hardest to forgive. A thing I could have fixed. Forty years of this and nobody has fixed the fan.
I said it to my aunt again at the end of a Thursday, with my shirt stuck to my back.
I said, Khaleh, if a man can't walk past my head without getting an idea, what exactly is wrong with me.
And she said, nothing is wrong with you.
And I said, then it is the men.
And she stopped with her hand on the light switch and she looked at me for a second longer than she needed to, and then she turned the light off and said, lock the back.
LONG, DYED A RED THAT IS NOT A HUMAN COLOUR, AND SHE LOVES IT.
I want to say what the shop was actually like, because if I only put the heavy things down it will come out as something it was not.
It was the funniest room I have ever been in.

The radio would be saying something about the currency and the second-Thursday woman would be saying it was the Americans and a woman under the dryer would be shouting that she could not hear and did anybody know whether the water was going off on Tuesday, and in the middle of all of it somebody would say one thing about somebody's son-in-law and the whole room would go. Properly go. Four women with wet heads laughing until one of them had to take her glasses off.

They talked about weddings for forty minutes at a time. Not the marriage. The catering. Who had been slighted over the seating. What a certain mother-in-law had worn and what she had said she had paid for it and what she had actually paid for it.

They talked about football. There was a woman who came in with her nephew's team's results written on the back of her hand because she could not keep them in her head and she wanted to be able to argue.

They talked about drivers. Everybody in that room held the same absolute conviction, which is that the drivers in this city are the worst in the world, and specifically the ones from one particular district, which would be named; and whoever in the room was from that district would say something unrepeatable; and off it would go again. In five years that was the only subject on which the shop reached unanimity, and it was wrong.
And the food. God. There would be an argument about rice that had been running for three visits.

I am putting this in because of a thing I noticed later. Of all the heads in my book, most of the second lines say nothing. Most of those women had not been stopped. Most of them went out in the morning with a scarf on their head the way you go out with shoes on your feet, and it did not cost them one thought, and they were perfectly happy, and they talked about catering.

The woman with the red hair came in that summer. It was a red that does not exist on any animal. She had been doing it for years and her daughters were embarrassed by it and she did not care in the slightest.
Her second line says nothing, except a fine for the car, which she said did not count because everybody gets those.

She was in the chair when the radio said something about a court and a sentence, and the room went quiet for about four seconds, and then she said, in that case I'm having it redder, and the whole shop fell apart.

I wrote her down laughing. I remember my handwriting on that one is bad because my hand was shaking from laughing, and for a long time afterwards I could not tell, looking at the page, whether my hand had been shaking from that or from the other thing.
SET, NOT CUT. THE SAME PARTING ON THE LEFT.
It was the first Saturday in Tir and it was the hottest day of that summer and the fan in the back had stopped working two days before and nobody had come to look at it.
Khanom Ansari came at ten with her money folded in her hand.

I had washed her head once a month for a year and a half by then and nothing had ever come. Not one thing. I had decided she was like the second-Thursday woman — that she had got all the way through and the rule had never put its hand on her — and I had decided it with a kind of relief, because I liked her.
That morning my hands were not right. It was the heat. I ran the water too hot and she said so, and I brought it down, and she settled her neck into the dip and shut her eyes.
And I put my hand flat on the back of her head, under the hair, which is a thing you do to lift it off the porcelain.
And it came in like a wall.

That she had worked in an office of a ministry. That she had been there nine years. That one morning the women were called in and told. That she did not have a scarf with her that day. That she was sent home at ten in the morning to fetch one. And that she was not let back in.
Twenty-two years of service. A pension she never drew one month of.
I stood there with my hand under her head and the water running over my wrist and did not move for long enough that she opened her eyes and looked up at me.
She said, what.

And I said nothing. I washed her hair and did the second wash and towelled her and walked her to the chair, and my aunt took over, and I went out into the yard and sat on the step in the forty degrees with my back against the wall.

Here is what she told me afterwards, in her own words, because I asked her. I went and sat down next to her at the mirrors while her set was going off and I said, Khanom Ansari, were you ever in an office.
And she looked at me in the glass for a second and then she told me, and it took about four minutes, and it is the only time in four and a half years that she said anything about herself.
She said: at the beginning nobody said it was compulsory.

She said: they said it was a recommendation. That is the word. A recommendation. There were women in the street about it and the answer that came back was that nobody had ordered anything, it was advice, and a great many people were satisfied with that, including me, because I wanted to be.

She said: by the next year you could not come through the door of the building without it. Not a rule on a wall. Nobody put up a notice. The man at the door simply did not let you through, and there was nobody to appeal to, because officially nothing had changed.

She said: and about four years after that it was the law. And I want you to understand, child, that not on one single day in those four years did anybody stand up anywhere and say, we have decided that the recommendation is now an order. There was no such day. I have looked for it my whole life. It does not exist.
She said: so that is how it happens. Not with an announcement. With a door.
I have thought about that sentence more than any other sentence anybody has said to me. Nobody in this country has ever been told anything. We have been let through doors, or not.
Then she said: and I was sent home at ten o'clock in the morning for a piece of cloth.
I said, but you came back the next day.
And she said, no.
I said, you went back, though. With a scarf. Everyone did.

And she said: I went back with a scarf. There was a different man at the door and my pass had been stopped and he was very polite about it. He said there was a letter coming. I waited for the letter for a year.
She said: I was thirty-one. I never worked again.
And then the dryer went on and she shut her eyes, and that was the end of it, and she came back on the first Saturday of the next month with her money folded in her hand.
THE PARTING AGAIN. IT HAS NOT MOVED IN FORTY YEARS.
There were two more things about Khanom Ansari and she did not tell me either of them. I had them from the water and then I watched for them for years afterwards and they were both true.
The first is the parting.
Forty years on the left, in the same line, never a centimetre either way. I had written it down a dozen times without once asking myself why a woman would do that.

Here is why. The last time she presented herself to the world looking different from the way she had looked the day before, she lost her entire working life before lunch. She went in at eight, she was on the street at ten, and she was never let back in.

So she never did it again. Not the parting, not the colour, not the length, not the coat. For forty years she has gone out of her front door looking exactly the way she looked the day before, and she has never been able to explain to anybody why, because she does not know it herself. She told my aunt once that she had never suited anything else, which is not true. I have seen a photograph.

That is what her hair kept. A head of hair grows about a centimetre a month, so there is a sense in which there is nothing left on her head that was there on that morning. It has all been replaced many times over. The hair is new. The line is not.
The second thing is the typing.
She cannot type.

There is nothing the matter with her hands. She knits, badly but at speed. She counts money like a teller. She can thread a needle without her glasses, at seventy, which my aunt could not do at fifty.

My cousin had an old machine, the kind with the carriage, and it sat on a table at a family thing one Friday, and Khanom Ansari was there, and somebody said, Khanom, you were a typist, show them. And she sat down at it.
And nothing happened.

She put her hands on it in the right position, with the thumbs where thumbs go, which showed that nine years were still in there somewhere. And then she sat with her hands on the keys and did not press any of them. For a while. Long enough that people stopped watching and started talking about something else to be kind.
Then she got up and said the ribbon was dry.
The ribbon was not dry. I checked afterwards, because I was that sort of child.

That is what her body kept. Not a bad back, not a scar, nothing anyone would write down anywhere. She simply cannot do the thing she was good at, forty years later, in a room full of her own family, on a Friday.
I wrote the two lines in the book that night at the kitchen table.
The parting again. It has not moved in forty years.
And she cannot type. Her hands are perfectly good.
And then I sat there for a long time, because I had just understood what I had in the drawer.

I had been writing down, for a year and a half, the first column. How long it was. What was in it. The thing anybody can see from the pavement, the thing the window is painted over for, the thing the law is about.

And the second column was what it had cost. And the second column was in nobody's book anywhere. Not in a court, not in an office, not in a newspaper. Khanom Ansari's twenty-two years are not written down in any building in this country. There is no file that says what that morning took. There is no number. Her pension is not a number that exists and was not paid; it is a thing that was never a number at all.
Except that it was now in a school exercise book with a cardboard cover, in a drawer under a till, in a shop with a painted window, in the handwriting of a girl of fifteen.
I would like somebody to explain to me how it is that the only ledger in this country with that figure in it was kept by a person who was not trusted to do a cut.
TO THE SHOULDER, AND SHE ASKED ME TO TAKE A HAND'S WIDTH OFF.
I did not tell anybody. I want to set down why, because at fifteen I thought about it quite hard and I think the reasons were the right ones even though they were not kind to me.
I did not tell my mother because my mother worked nights and when she was home she slept, and because the one thing my mother wanted was for me to be a girl with no complications.

I did not tell my aunt because of the night in the yard with the barrel. I had seen what she did with eighteen years of names. I understood, in a way I could not have put in words, that in that family you did not hand someone a thing they would then have to carry.
And I did not tell a friend because I was fifteen and I knew exactly what would happen. It would be a game by Thursday.
So I kept it, and the keeping of it is the thing that actually changed me, more than the knowing.

Because it is useless. I cannot warn anybody; there is nothing to warn them about, it has already happened. I cannot prove anything, and I cannot help one single woman with it, and I cannot even talk to them about it, because the one thing every one of them has in common is that they did not choose to tell me.
It only works backwards. It tells me the price after it has been paid, when there is nothing left to do about the price. I have been given the one talent in the world that is purely administrative.
And it does not get easier. People say you get used to things. I got worse.

And it only ever happens with women, because women are the only people I wash. There is a barber two doors down with a striped pole and I have never once been inside it. So everything in my book is one-sided. Everything in it was paid by one half of the people on my street.
I have thought about that a great deal and I have never once wished I could read the other half.

The woman that Saturday had three daughters and she asked me to take a hand's width off because of the heat, and my aunt let me do the cut, which was the first one she ever let me do, and it was not good but it was not bad.
Two of her daughters had cost her nothing. Nothing at all, not a stop, not a word.

And the third one was there and would not come near the water, and sat by the door the whole time with her bag on her knees looking at the painted window, and did not take her scarf off, inside, in a women's shop, in Tir, in forty degrees.
I did not write her down. She was not a head. She was a girl sitting by a door.
I have thought since that she is the only person in the entire book who got away from me, and that she is probably the reason I kept going.
ALL ONE LENGTH, TO THE JAW, GROWN OUT AND LEFT.
The last Thursday in Mordad we shut at nine and the street was still warm enough that the shutters ticked when they came down.
We walked home the long way because my aunt wanted cigarettes and the man on the corner by the bakery is the only one who still sells them singly.
I had my scarf on. She had hers on. Everybody on that pavement had hers on; it was not a thing you noticed any more than you notice that the cars are on the right.

She smoked about a third of it and gave the rest to a man sitting on the step outside the pharmacy, which she did every time, and which in five years neither of them ever mentioned. I have watched two people conduct an entire relationship on two-thirds of a cigarette.
And she said, how is the book.
I said, fine.
She said, how many.
I said I did not know, a few hundred, and she said, hm.
And I said, Khaleh, why do you want me to do it.
And she said: I don't want you to do it. I want it done.

That is exactly what she said. I have had four years to decide what it meant and I had it wrong for all four of them. At fifteen I thought she was being my aunt — that it was one of those jobs adults invent for you, like counting the towels, so that you have something to be in charge of.

Her own hair was all one length to the jaw that summer, grown out from the night in the bathroom with the kitchen scissors and left alone, and when I washed it, which I did every second week for four years, nothing came. Nothing at all. In four years I never got one single fact about my aunt out of the water, and I decided that this meant she was like the second-Thursday woman.

I was fifteen and I had a book in a drawer with a few hundred heads in it, and under more than half of them it said nothing, and under the rest of them it said things like a morning, and a van, and twenty-two years.
I did not know yet that it was a bill. I thought it was a list.

And I did not know why my aunt cut her hair to that exact length, or why she had it cut to that exact length again six weeks later, and again six weeks after that, and again, and again, for every year I was in that shop, and why she would stand at the mirror afterwards with her head slightly on one side and look at it for a moment too long, and then say, right, and go and put the kettle on.
I watched her do that perhaps forty times. I never once asked.
II. THE SECOND COLUMN

There was a woman who came in on Mondays who had taught for thirty years, and one Monday in Dey she said a thing to me very quietly, with the dryer going two chairs down, and then never said anything like it again for the rest of the time I knew her.
I had asked her my question. By then I asked everybody. I had got used to the laughing.
She did not laugh. She looked at the mirror and not at me and she said: do you know what the book actually says.
I said I thought I did.
She said: there are two places. In one of them it says that women should draw their coverings over their chests. In the other it says they should be known, so that they are not troubled.
She said: that is it. That is the whole of it. Two places.
Then she said: now tell me which word in either of those is the word for hair.
I did not say anything.
She said: there isn't one. The word is not there. Not in the first and not in the second. You can look. People do look. It is not a secret and it is not a trick.

She said: hair came afterwards. Men who studied the law for a living worked it out later, out of other things, and some of them disagreed with each other, and some of them leaned on a report that other scholars — their own, not foreigners — have argued about ever since on the grounds that the chain of people who passed it down does not hold up.

She said: and that argument has never been settled. It is not settled now. There are people of faith in this very city, good ones, who will tell you the hair was never in it, and there are people of faith who will tell you it obviously was, and both of them can give you their reasons, and I am not going to tell you which of them is right because I do not know.
Then she said: I am telling you that it is an argument. That is all I am telling you. Most people your age are brought up to think it is not one.
And then she said, in a completely different voice: is that water going cold?
It was not going cold. I turned it anyway.

Three weeks later I washed her hair and found out what it had cost her, in her life, over thirty years, to be a woman who knew that and mostly did not say it. And she had not told me and never did tell me, and I never once let on.
TO THE SHOULDER, GOING GREY AT THE TEMPLES AND SHE IS LETTING IT.
I was fifteen when school started again and by then the book had two lines on every page and I had worked out how to do it.

You do not write it at the basin. You cannot; your hands are wet and there is a woman in front of you with her eyes shut. You carry it. You carry it up to the chair and you hand her over and you go to the till and you write two lines while the dryer runs, and it takes about forty seconds, and then you go and do the next one.
The first line I write straight. How long, what colour, what was in it, what she asked for.
The second line I write as short as I can get it.

I found that out by accident. In the beginning I wrote the second line properly, in sentences, the way you would tell somebody. And after a few weeks I could not read my own pages without having to put the book down. So I cut them. Not to hide anything — the book is not in code, anybody could read it — but because a morning is something you can write and four days is something you can write, and the long version is something you have to live through again at the till with a dryer going.

So the second column of that book is the shortest writing I have ever done. Some of it is one word. I have since been told that this is a style. It is not a style. It is what you can get down before you have to look up and smile at somebody.
Nothing.
That is the most common entry in the whole book. I want to keep saying that because it is true and because it is the thing I would not have believed before I started.

More than half of the women who sat in that chair had never been stopped, never been spoken to, never had a hand put on them, never been photographed, never had a letter, never had a message. They went out in the morning with a scarf on the way you go out with shoes on. It cost them nothing. They were not brave and they were not cowards; it had simply never come up.
And there is no way to tell them apart. That is the thing. You cannot look at a room of six women with wet heads and see which two of them are the ones.
Which I would like to put beside something the radio says often, which is that a person who has done nothing has nothing to fear. I have a book that proves the opposite with dates in it.
The woman that first Monday was letting the grey come in at the temples, deliberately, against her daughter's advice, which she reported to the whole shop with great satisfaction.
Her second line says nothing.

I wrote it and I was glad, and then I noticed that I had been glad, and that noticing is the thing that changed me more than any of it. Because to be glad that a page says nothing is to have accepted what the other pages are.
LONG, AND SHE HAD IT UP ALL DAY FOR WORK AND WANTED IT DOWN.
That autumn they arrested a girl for dancing.

She was about my age, maybe a year older. She had been putting up short films of herself dancing in her bedroom, the way everybody does, hundreds of them, nothing in them at all. And they took her, and they put her on the television saying she was sorry.
I watched it with the sound off because the sound is always off in the shop. You could see her face.

I would like somebody to walk me through the meeting. Because a room of adults sat down with a problem, and the problem was that a schoolgirl had danced in her bedroom, and the solution they arrived at was national broadcast.

And then over the next days women started putting up films of themselves dancing. Thousands of them. Old women. Women in kitchens. A woman in a hospital uniform in a corridor. Two sisters in a garden with a hose going. My own cousin, who cannot dance.

Nobody organised it. I want to be accurate about that, because at the time it felt like something enormous, like a thing with a shape, and years later I went looking for who had started it and there is no answer. There is no name. Somebody did it and then somebody else did it.

They spent a television channel on one girl and got back several thousand girls. If a week went like that in our shop my aunt would have shut early and gone through the order book to find out where it had gone wrong.
The shop was split and it was split in a way I did not expect.
The second-Thursday woman said the girl was a fool and that her mother must be dying of it.
A woman whose name I never got said what exactly do you expect them to do, they cannot have every girl in the country in her bedroom on a telephone.
And a woman in the end chair, who was about sixty and had said nothing all morning, said: when I was that age they would not have put her on the television. They would have just kept her.
And the room went quiet, because that was true, and because nobody wanted it to be the thing that was said.
Then somebody asked about the water going off on Tuesday and it went again.

Nobody won. Nobody in that shop in five years ever won one of those. The same six opinions, in different mouths, for four and a half years, and not one of them ever got within a mile of a person who could do anything about any of it.

The woman at the basin that day had kept a warning letter for years in a tin. It was not even hers. It had come about her brother. She had kept it because it had her family's name on it and she did not trust herself to remember the exact wording.
SHORT AND PRACTICAL, AND SHE HAS WORN IT LIKE THAT SINCE SHE WAS FORTY.
Three weeks after she told me about the two verses, I washed the teacher's hair.
She came on Mondays at twenty past ten and she had a bad hip and she liked the water hotter than anybody else in the book.

And what came was not an event. That is why this one is in here. There is no van and no morning and no letter. There is no moment at all. What came was thirty years of a woman keeping her mouth almost shut, and the two times she did not.

The first time was early and she was young and it was not even about this. It was about a text she had taken out of a lesson because she thought it was too hard for the class, and somebody reported that she had taken it out, and she was moved to another school across the city with an hour and a half each way.
The second time was years later and I do not know what she said, because what came to me was not the words. What came was the transfer, and the room.

They moved her to an administrative post. That is the phrase. She kept her salary and her grade and her thirty years of service, and she was put in a room at the back of a building with no window in it, to check lists.
For six years.
And then she asked to go back to a classroom and they let her, without a word about any of it, as though the six years had been a thing she had chosen.

That is what her body kept, and it is the quietest thing in the book and I think it is one of the worst. She does not finish sentences in front of people she does not know. She starts them and then she does a thing with her hand, a small flick, and lets you finish it yourself. Everyone who knows her thinks it is a manner. It is not a manner. It is a woman who learned, in a room with no window, that an unfinished sentence cannot be reported.
She had told me the thing about the two verses with her eyes on the mirror and the dryer going two chairs away, in about ninety seconds, and then she had asked about the water.

I understand now what that cost and what it was. She was sixty-one years old and she had been moved twice and shut in a room for six years, and she looked at a girl of fifteen with her hands in a basin and decided to spend some of what she had left on telling her that a thing she had been raised to believe was settled was in fact an argument.

And her hair keeps it, in the dullest way imaginable. She has worn it short and practical since she was forty. Easy to do herself. Nothing anybody could comment on. Not one single feature of that woman's appearance has ever given anybody anything to write down.

I did not thank her. I did not say anything at all, ever, about any of it. She would have hated it, and more than that, it would have told her that someone had worked it out, and she had spent thirty years making sure nobody could.
TO THE MIDDLE OF HER BACK AND SHE HAS NEVER CUT IT SHORTER THAN THAT.
I was stopped for the first time in Esfand, two weeks before the new year, on the pavement outside the fruit shop on our street, with a bag of oranges.
I was fifteen.
A woman in a chador and a man a little way behind her. The woman did the talking. She was not angry and she did not shout and she was not even unkind. She was about thirty-five and she sounded tired.
My scarf had gone back off my hairline, which happens, because it happens to everybody about forty times a day.
She said, sister, fix your scarf.
And I said sorry, and I fixed it.
And she said, God keep you, and they went on.
That is all of it. Eight seconds. I stood there with the oranges and my heart going like a bird, and then I went home and did not tell anybody.

I have gone over it since and the detail I keep arriving at is that she was working. She was out in Esfand, in the cold, on a Thursday, doing a shift. Somebody pays for that. There is a line in a budget in this country for a woman to stand outside a fruit shop and ask a girl of fifteen to move four centimetres of cloth, and the water on our street goes off on Tuesdays.
And here is the thing I need to put in, because it is the only part of it that is interesting.

It cost me nothing. Nothing at all. It is not in my book, because I am not in my book. If somebody had handed me an exercise book and told me to write down what my own head had cost me, I would have written nothing, and I would have been right.
But I was frightened for two days. I changed which way I walked to the bus for a month. I checked the mirror by the door in a way I had not before.
So it cost me something that does not go in a column.

The second time was in Farvardin, after the new year, and it was a man in a car who leaned over and said something out of the window and drove on, and it was not official in any way, and I have thought a great deal about why that one made me angrier.

I think it is because the woman in Esfand was doing a job. There was a thing she was for. I could see the shape of it. The man in the car was just a man in a car who had been told his whole life that my head was a matter he had standing in.

My aunt knew about the first one within a week. I do not know how. She did not ask me about it. What she did was start sending me on errands at different times of day, and she did it for about two months, and then she stopped, and she never once said why.

The woman at the basin that week had hair to the middle of her back and had never in her life cut it shorter. Her line says nothing. She wanted it put on the record — not my record, she did not know about my record, just said out loud to the room — that her husband was a good man and had never once in thirty-one years said one word to her about what she wore.
Several women in the room said, mine neither.
And one said nothing at all and looked at the floor, and I had washed her hair the month before, and I knew why.
THIN AT THE LEFT TEMPLE. IT STILL HAS NOT CAUGHT UP.
The woman in the green coat came back in Ordibehesht, a year and a month after the first time, and asked for me by name.

My aunt told me afterwards that she had been in twice in between and had sat in the chair for a cut and gone away without a wash both times, and had paid the full price both times and would not be talked out of it.
Her name was Hengameh. She was forty-four.
She sat down at the basin and she leaned straight back, no waiting, and she said: all right. Go on then.

And I washed her hair, and this time it came whole, and I am going to put it down the way I eventually got it, some of it from the water and some of it from her own mouth over the next two years, because she did tell me in the end. She is the only one who ever did.

It was years before I met her. She was in her thirties. She was coming out of a shop on a main road at about four in the afternoon with a plastic bag in her hand and there was a van at the kerb and two women and a man.
What she had on her head was a scarf. It was on her head. It was back off the hairline, the way mine was outside the fruit shop, the way everybody's is.
They asked for her identity card and she gave it to them, and then they said to get in.

She said, I remember asking if I could telephone my husband, and they said from the station, and I said what station, and nobody answered me, because there was no station. There was never a station. We drove around.
She was in that van for three hours.
And I need to say what she said next exactly, because she said it twice, a year apart, in the same words, which is how you know.
She said: nothing happened to me in the van.

She said: I want that understood. Nobody hit me. Nobody said anything filthy to me. There were four of us in the back by the end and the youngest one was crying and one of the women gave her a tissue out of her own bag.
She said: the only thing that happened is that when I would not get in, the man took hold of my hair at the side, here, through the scarf, and used it. Not hard. The way you move a chair.

Then they drove around for three hours and at some point she signed a paper that she did not read and was not given a copy of, and then at about seven in the evening they stopped the van and let her out.
On the same corner. The same one she had been picked up on. With her bag of shopping still in it.
She said: and that is the part nobody understands. They brought me back. Three hours of my life and then they put me down exactly where they found me, like a cat.
And then she went home.
And her husband was in the kitchen, and he had been telephoning her for three hours, and he turned round, and the first thing out of his mouth was:
What were you wearing?
AND SHE HAS LET SOMEBODY ELSE DO IT NOW. FIRST TIME IN THIRTEEN YEARS.
Here is what Hengameh's hair kept.

A patch at the left temple, about the size of a thumbprint, where the hair came back thinner and never caught up. Thirteen years. It is not bald and nobody would see it. It is thinner than the other side and it always will be, and she combs the front across it without thinking about it, the way you favour a knee.
And this, which is the real thing, and which I did not understand the size of until I was older.
She had not let another human being wash her hair in thirteen years.

Not a shop. Not her mother. Not her husband. She did it herself, at her own kitchen sink, with a jug, twice a week, for thirteen years, because the one thing she could not have was somebody standing behind her with their hands in her hair while she had her eyes shut and her neck back.

So when she came in the first time in that green coat, and stood just inside the door for too long, and sat forward with her hands in her lap and looked at the taps — that was a woman who had been working up to it, on and off, for thirteen years. And she came back twice and paid for a wash she did not have. And then she came back a third time and asked for me, and leaned straight back, and said go on then.
I was fifteen. I had no idea. I thought I was washing a nervous woman's hair.
And what her body kept is two things, and they are both small and neither of them is on any paper anywhere.
She cannot hear a diesel engine idling. Not a moving one. A stopped one. She will cross a street. She has crossed a street with me and said nothing about it and I said nothing either.

And she does not look at herself in the windows of parked cars. Everyone does that. Everyone in the world does that, a hundred times a week, without knowing. She does not. Her eyes go past it. I have watched her do it for years.
Now here is the arithmetic, and I did not do this arithmetic at fifteen. I did it much later, at the till, with the book open, going backwards through it.

What it cost her: a patch of her scalp, three hours, thirteen years of washing her own hair at a sink, two streets she cannot walk down, and the honest ground of her marriage. She says her marriage is fine, and I believe her, and she is right. It is a good marriage. It is just not the marriage it was at a quarter to seven that evening, because at seven o'clock she found out what the first thing he thought was.
And what it bought them — the van, the three hours, the paper she signed and never read:
She was out again, scarf back off her hairline, same as the rest of us, within four months.
She told me that herself and she laughed when she said it. She said: what were they expecting? I have one head.
DOWN TO HER WAIST, AND SHE IS NINETEEN AND HAS NEVER HAD IT CUT.
That summer the radio said a number and the shop stopped.
A woman had been sentenced. The total was twenty-four years. And of the twenty-four, fifteen of them were for taking her scarf off in public.
Fifteen years.

I was sixteen and I did the thing you do, which is to count forward. I would be thirty-one. The girl at the basin that afternoon, who was nineteen and wanted to be a dentist, would be thirty-four. Khanom Ansari would be eighty-five and would almost certainly not be alive.
Nobody in that room said anything for a while. Then the woman under the dryer shouted what, and somebody told her, and she said God preserve us, and then — I remember this exactly — she said, well.
Well.
And that was the whole of the shop's response to fifteen years. One syllable, from a woman with her head under a dryer, who could not hear.
I was angry about that for a long time. I thought it was cowardice, or that it was the thing where people stop being able to feel a number after a while.

It was not either of those. I understand it now. There was nothing to say. There was no sentence available in that room that would have done anything at all. You cannot be sufficiently appalled. There is no quantity of appalled that reaches a courtroom; it is not a currency they accept. So you say well, and then you ask about the water on Tuesday, because the water on Tuesday is the only item on the agenda that anybody in that room has standing on.
But here is the part that matters, and it took me years to see it, and I only saw it because of the book.

Khanom Ansari lost twenty-two years of her life over a scarf she did not have with her, and the state did not have to spend anything to take it. No van. No file. No court. One man at a door, politely, and a letter that never came. It cost them a morning's inconvenience and it bought them a ministry full of obedient women for years.

And now they were spending fifteen years in a courtroom, in public, on paper, with a number that went around the world — and the girl at my basin, nineteen years old, who had heard the radio the same as the rest of us, came back six weeks later with her hair down to her waist and her scarf in her bag.

Not out of defiance. She did not make a speech. I asked her about it, actually, because I was sixteen and rude, and she said: oh, it's so hot, and I forget, and nobody says anything any more on our street.
Nobody says anything any more on our street.
They paid fifteen years in the most expensive, most public, most carefully recorded way they had ever paid for it.
And what they got for it was a nineteen-year-old on a bus with her scarf in her bag saying nobody says anything any more.
I did not have a word for what I was looking at. I was sixteen. The word I have for it now I got from my mother, and she got it from standing in a queue, and I will come to it.
CUT TO THE JAW SIX WEEKS AGO. CUT TO THE JAW AGAIN TONIGHT.
My mother came off nights for one week in Tir and slept for three days and then on the fourth day she took me to buy shoes.
The shoes were a certain price. She looked at them and put them down and said something I have never forgotten, which is: last year this was the same number and it was a different shoe.
I said I did not understand.
And she said: the number did not change, Baran. The shoe got worse. That is how they do it. They do not tell you the money is worth less. They put less in the bag and leave the number on the front.

Everybody in this country knows that in their hands. You do not need to have been to school for it. You know it from bread. You know that the note in your pocket says what it said last year and will not buy what it bought last year, and that nobody announced that, and that nobody will ever announce it, and that there is no day on which it happened.
Hold on to that. It is the only idea in this book that is mine, and I got it in a shoe shop, which I think is where most of the good ones are.
That night I washed my aunt's hair, which I did every second week, and I wrote nothing on the second line the way I had written nothing on the second line about her for two years.

Earlier in the day she had cut her own hair, at the mirror, to the jaw. All one length. She had done it six weeks before and she did it that night and she would do it again in six weeks, and she had been doing it for as long as I had known her.
And afterwards she stood and looked at it with her head a little on one side, the way she always did, for about three seconds longer than a person looks at a haircut.
And then she said, right. And went and put the kettle on.
I had watched her do that, by then, something like twenty times.

I remember being mildly irritated that night, because I had wanted to try something with the front and she would not let me, and she was not even rude about it, she just said no, this length, and held up two fingers at her jaw, and that was the end of it.

I have gone back over that evening more times than any other evening in this book. There is nothing in it. We ate. She watched her serial. I did my homework at the kitchen table with the book in my bag and did not take it out.

She was fifty-two years old and she had already paid more than everybody else in my book put together, and I had my hands in her hair twice a month for five years and the water never told me one single thing about her, and I decided that this meant she had got off lightly.
NOT WASHED. SHE CAME IN TO SIT DOWN.
In Aban they put the price of fuel up overnight and the country came out into the road.

It was not about scarves. I want that in here, because everything in this book is about one thing and that week was not. It was about the price of fuel, and behind the price of fuel it was about the money, and behind the money it was about forty years, and there were men in it and boys in it and women in it and the whole street.
Then the internet went off.
Not slow. Off. For days. And when a country of that size has its internet turned off for days, what you have is a place where nobody can find out what is happening three streets away.
The shop did not open for three days. My aunt took the key with her and did not say anything about when.
And on the fourth day she opened it, and nobody came, and we sat in there with the radio on and the painted window and the licence in the frame and did not do one head all morning.
A woman came in at about two in the afternoon and did not want her hair washed. She sat down in the second chair with her coat on and asked for a glass of water.
