She had a son. He had gone out on the second night and had not come back and it was now the fourth day and she did not know which hospital to go to, because when you do not know whether a person is in a hospital or somewhere else, every question you ask is also a piece of information about you.

She sat in that chair for about forty minutes. My aunt sat in the next one. Neither of them said very much. At one point my aunt held her hand, which I had never seen her do with a customer in two years.

I did not wash her hair. There is a line in my book for that day and the first column says not washed, she came in to sit down, which is the only time that appears, and the second column says what I have put at the top of this entry, and I wrote it from her face and her voice and not from the water, which means that by the standards of the rest of the book it should not be in there at all.
I left it in. It is still in. I decided at sixteen that it was going in and I have never changed my mind.

He was alive. I want to say that straight away because of what it is like to read it otherwise. He came home eight days later with his arm in a sling and a story about a friend's house that nobody in his family has ever contradicted and nobody in his family believes.
But I did not know that for eight days, and neither did she, and neither did my aunt, who sat in a chair holding the hand of a woman she had been doing hair for since before I was born.
And my aunt did not sleep that week, and asked me twice, in a voice she did not usually use, to come and sit in the front room while she watched the television.
I thought she was frightened for the street. I was sixteen. I thought it was about the street.
TO THE SHOULDER. THE PARTING. SHE IS SEVENTY-TWO NOW.
Khanom Ansari came on the first Saturday of Azar with her money folded in her hand and the internet had been back for a week and nobody in the shop would talk about Aban at all.

That is a thing I should put down. There was no argument about Aban. There was no six opinions in six mouths. The money got argued about every week for four and a half years, and the dancing got argued about, and the sentence got a well out of a woman under a dryer.
Aban got nothing. The room went around it the way you go around a hole in a pavement, without looking down, for months.
I washed her hair. The parting was where it has always been. She was seventy-two.
And then with her eyes shut she said: how old are you now.
I said sixteen.
And she said: and what are you going to do.
I said I did not know. Which was true. I was sixteen and I liked chemistry and I was frightened of the examination the way everybody is frightened of the examination.
And she said: not that. I mean what are you going to do.

And I knew exactly what she meant, because she had told me about the hot pitch in my first week and she had told me about the man at the door and the letter that never came, and she was asking me whether I was going to spend my life the way she had spent hers, which is to say carefully.
And I said: I don't know, Khanom Ansari.

Which was a lie. I did know. What I knew was that I had a book in a drawer six feet from where she was lying with her neck in the porcelain, and that her twenty-two years were on page something-or-other of it in my handwriting, and that if anybody ever found that book I did not know what would happen but I knew it would not be nothing.
I had known that for about a year by then and I had not stopped writing it, and I had not asked my aunt why she wanted it, and I had not told one single person alive.
So the honest answer to what are you going to do was: I am already doing it, every day, at forty seconds a head, and I do not know what it is for.
I said I don't know, and she said hm, and I turned the water off, and I walked her up to the chair.
Four and a half years, and that is the only question she ever asked me.
LONG, AND THE ENDS ARE WRECKED, AND SHE WILL NOT HAVE THEM OFF.
Towards the end of that year a man came round the shops on our street with a clipboard and a lanyard and went into four of them and not into ours.

My aunt watched him through the gap at the edge of the painted window for about twenty minutes. He went into the carpet place, the bakery, the shop that sells plastic, and the pharmacy. Not ours. I have never seen my aunt so insulted by being left out of something she was frightened of.

She did not say anything to me about it that day. What she did was go round the shop in the evening after we had shut and check things. The frame on the wall, straight. The licence in date. The curtain on the rail, which she pulled all the way across and let go and pulled again. The gap at the edge of the paint where the brush had not quite reached the frame, which she went over with a fresh tin on the Friday, herself, standing on a chair, at fifty-two years old, with me holding the chair.
I said, Khaleh, it is one corner, nobody can see anything through it.
And she said: that is not the point.
I said, what is the point.
And she said: the point is that if a man comes in here with a clipboard I want there to be nothing at all for him to write down. Not one thing. Not a corner, not a date, not a cup in the sink.
I have thought about that sentence as much as any sentence in this book.

Because she painted over a corner of a window she had already painted, standing on a chair, at fifty-two, to stop a man writing down a true thing about a corner. That is not fear of being punished. There was nothing to punish. It is a different thing and I did not have a word for it then.
Because she was not frightened of being punished for something she had done. There was nothing to punish. The paint was fine and the licence was in date and the shop was clean.
She was frightened of being written down.

The woman at the basin that week had a business, a little one, printing on cloth, with four women working for her. The lease was in her brother's name. Everything was in her brother's name. She was the one who did all of it and she was on no piece of paper anywhere, on purpose, and had arranged her entire working life that way, and when I washed her hair what came was not an arrest or a fine or a van.
What came was a woman who had made herself, carefully, over twenty years, into somebody with nothing in her own name.

That is not a punishment. Nobody did it to her. There is no court anywhere that ordered it. It is what she worked out, by herself, from watching, and it has cost her her whole legal existence, and she will tell you it was simply the sensible thing.
Her ends were wrecked from a bad colour and she would not let my aunt take them off because she had been growing it since her mother died.
TWO HUNDRED AND SIX HEADS SINCE DEY OF THE YEAR BEFORE LAST.
On the last night of Esfand I counted the book. Two hundred and six heads, and eighty-one of them with something in the second column.

Then I tried to add the second column up, and found out that you cannot. A morning and a van and three hours and twenty-two years and a room with no window are not the same kind of thing and there is no unit they all go into.
But I could see the shape of it, and the shape is what frightened me, and it is this.
Every single one of those eighty-one women paid it on her own.

Not one of them knew another one. I had them in a book, so I knew, which makes me the only person on earth who did know. Khanom Ansari did not know about Hengameh. Hengameh did not know about the teacher. The teacher did not know about the woman with the business in her brother's name, and that woman had been coming to that shop for six years and had sat in a chair next to at least four of the others and had talked to them about rice.

There was no one organising any of it. There was no list anywhere. Nobody had told any of them that what was being done to them was also being done to a hundred other women inside two kilometres of the same street. Each of them thought it was her own bad luck, or her own fault, or her own carelessness about a scarf on a hairline on an ordinary afternoon.

And on the other side there was no list either. The van was police. The morning was a man at a door in a ministry. The clipboard was from the municipality. The room with no window was the education office. Fifteen years was a court. A message is sent by something else again.

No two of them have to agree. No two of them ever did agree. That is why the second-Thursday woman went fifty-nine years and was never touched once and Hengameh was put in a van for a scarf on a hairline, on the same street, in the same city, under the same rule.

It is not a machine. I spent a year looking for the machine. There is no machine. There are a great many separate offices, each with its own paper, and none of them has ever added up what the others have taken, and there is no office anywhere whose job that is.

Which means the thing I had been imagining for a year — a room, a man, a list — does not exist, and I was almost disappointed, the way you are when you find out the person who has been ruining your life is not even thinking about you.
I was sixteen. I put the book back in my bag.

Then I went and stood in the doorway of the front room, where my aunt had fallen asleep in the chair with the serial on and the sound down, with her hair cut to the jaw, all one length, exactly the way it had been six weeks before and exactly the way it would be in another six.
And I did not know one single thing about her.
III. WHAT IT COST
There was a woman who had been a nurse in another country for twenty years and had come back to look after her father, and she had opinions about everything and no patience with any of us.
I asked her my question in the second year of the sickness, when we were all in masks and she was the only person in the shop who wore hers properly.
She said: you think this is a Muslim thing.
I said I had never said that.
She said: good, because it isn't, and I will tell you what I know and then you can go and find out the rest yourself, because nobody is going to hand it to you.

She said: the Greeks did it. The Romans did it. In the old Jewish law a married woman who went out with her head uncovered could be divorced and her husband did not have to pay her a thing. There is a letter in the Christian book telling women to cover their heads in church, and the reason it gives — she stopped here and laughed — the reason it gives is because of the angels. Go and look it up. Because of the angels.
She said: and all of those people were doing it before anybody in this part of the world had heard of our religion. It arrived into a place where it was already being done. It did not bring it.
And then she said the thing I did not expect from her, because she was not a sentimental woman.

She said: and do you know what is strange? If you look at the old pictures — the statues, the floors in the old houses, the ones with the little tiles — most of the women do not have anything on their heads. The priests were shouting about it for three hundred years and you look at the pictures and most of them are bare. And in the ones where a rich woman has a beautiful cloth on her head, the girl standing next to her holding the jug has nothing. The cloth was not modesty. The cloth was so you could tell which of them was the lady.
Then she washed her hands, although I was the one with my hands in the basin, and she said:
I will tell you why it is always hair, and then I am going to stop talking about it, because it upsets me.

She said: I worked for twenty years in a ward. When somebody is going, you cut a piece of their hair and you put it in an envelope and you write the name on the front and you give it to the family. I have done it hundreds of times. Nobody asks you to and everybody wants it.
She said: now think about why it is the hair and not anything else.

She said: because it is the only part of a person you can take off them and hand to somebody else, and it does not hurt them, and it is still them. That is all. That is the whole reason, and it is four thousand years old, and it is why it ended up in a law.
Then she said, is that hot enough, and I said yes, and she did not say another word about any of it for the rest of the time I knew her.
TO THE SHOULDER. SHE ASKED FOR IT SHORTER THAN USUAL, IN CASE.
In Farvardin of the next year they shut everything, and the shop was shut for most of three months.
The last Wednesday before we shut, a woman came in and asked for it shorter than she liked it, in case, and that is the only thing anybody said out loud all day about what was coming. In case.
Then the shutters came down and stayed down.
I want to put in what that did to the book, because it is the only thing that happened to the book that I did not do myself.
There is a page in the middle of it with a date at the top and then nothing underneath, and then the next date is most of three months later. A gap. The only gap in five years.
And when we opened again, every single head that came through that door was wrong.

Long. All of them. Grown out, every colour gone two or three centimetres up from the root, cuts that had been cut in winter sitting on women in summer, grey everywhere — grey on women I had never once seen with grey, because they had been coming to that shop every four weeks for twenty years and I had genuinely never seen them.
My aunt stood in the middle of the shop on the first morning, looked at the four of them waiting, and said: God. Look at us.

They had shut the shops, the schools, the offices and the shrines, in that order, and the shrines went last and went hardest, and in the middle of it somebody somewhere was still having to decide whether a hairdresser counts. I would pay money to read that file.
And a woman in the second chair said: this is what we actually look like.

Everybody laughed. It was funny. It was also the truest thing said in that shop in five years and I wrote it down on a separate piece of paper and kept it in the back of the book, which I had never done before.
This is what we actually look like.

The first column of my book for that month is useless. Useless. I had been measuring something for two years and then the thing I was measuring was suspended for most of three months and came back unrecognisable, and the only reason was that the shops were shut.
If anybody had ever looked at my book to find out something about the women of that district, the gap would have told them nothing except that there was a sickness.
But it told me something, and it is the first thing I understood on my own without anybody saying it to me.
The first column was never about the women. It was about the shop. It was a record of a service. Who got in, how often, and what the trade could do for them.
The second column was the only part of that book that was about the women themselves.
GREY ALL ALONG THE PARTING AND SHE IS LEAVING IT NOW.
Then for about a year and a half everybody in the country covered their face.
I was seventeen and I want to be careful here, because I have heard people say clever things about this and most of them are too clever.

It was not the same. A mask is not a scarf. Nobody was ever put in a van for a mask. The reason for a mask was a sickness, and the sickness was real, and I had a great-aunt who died of it in Ramadan and we could not go.
But something happened in that shop that I still think about.

The radio told us to cover our faces. There were signs on the bus and the bank and the bakery. There were men at doors not letting people in. For a year and a half, the whole machinery of this country — the radio, the signs, the men at the doors, the fines — was pointed at getting everybody to put a thing over the middle of their face.
And a lot of people did not do it. They wore it under the chin. They wore it on the wrist. They pulled it up when they went past a man at a door and pulled it down afterwards.

And I stood at the basin and watched a room full of women who had spent their entire lives pulling a scarf forward when they went past a man at a door, and pulling it back afterwards, do exactly the same thing with a mask, with exactly the same hand, in exactly the same movement.
They were extremely good at it. They had forty years of practice.

So the one thing this country has successfully taught every woman in it, at enormous expense, over four decades, is how to appear to comply. That is the national competence. We are world-class. If there were a competition we would send a team.
The second-Thursday woman said something that week that was the most intelligent thing she ever said in that shop, and she said it while complaining, which is how most intelligent things get said.
She said: they have taught us to do this. Forty years of making us cover something has taught every woman in this country how to look like she is obeying and not obey.
And then she said she still was not wearing it on the bus because it made her glasses go.

Nobody won that argument either. The woman in the next chair said the sickness was a lie and her cousin was a pharmacist. The teacher, who was in that morning, said nothing and did the thing with her hand.
That was the year I started to see the second column differently, and it was because of the masks and because of my mother's shoe.

Here is what I had. Khanom Ansari had lost twenty-two years to one morning and one piece of cloth, and it had cost the state one polite man at a door. Hengameh had lost thirteen years of letting anybody near her head, and it had cost them a van and an afternoon and four men's wages. Fifteen years in a courtroom had bought them a nineteen-year-old with her scarf in her bag.
The price they were paying was going up. And what they were getting for it was going down.
I did not have the word. My mother had the word, from the shoe shop, and I was still a year away from putting the two together.
SHORT, GREY, AND SHE HAS NEVER DYED IT AND NEVER WILL.
The nurse came in on a Thursday at the end of that summer with her father's prescriptions in her bag, sat down, and said, you again.

She had worked abroad for twenty years and she could not stop comparing, and she knew she should stop, and she did not. Somebody once asked her how she found things since she came back and she thought about it and said, warmer.

She had been in four or five times by then. She was sixty and she had been away for twenty years and had come back, and she had the thing people have when they have lived somewhere else, which is that she could not stop comparing and knew she should stop and did not.

That was the Thursday she told me about the Greeks and the Romans and the law about a married woman's head, and the letter about the angels, and the pictures where the rich woman has the cloth and the girl with the jug has nothing.
And then she told me about the envelopes.

She said she had cut hair off people in a ward hundreds of times and put it in an envelope and written the name on the front and given it to a family, and that nobody had ever asked her to do it and everybody had wanted it.
And then she said: that is why it is always hair. It is the only part of a person you can take off them and hand to somebody else, and it does not hurt them, and it is still them.

I stood there with the water running and I understood about four things at once, and I am going to try to put them down in the order they arrived, because it is the only time in this whole book that I worked something out instead of being handed it.
The first was that she was right and that it was obvious and that nobody had ever said it to me.

The second was that this is why it is in the law. Not because it is beautiful and not because men are weak. Because it is the one piece of a person that works as a sign. You can put a cloth over it. You can take it away. You can measure it, which is what I had been doing for two and a half years. It is the part of a body that behaves like a thing.

The third was that this is why I could read it. I did not say that out loud and I have never said it out loud. But a head of hair grows about a centimetre a month and it does not throw anything away, and I had a drawer full of pages proving that it keeps a record, and the nurse had just told me, without knowing what she was telling me, why it would be hair and not an elbow.
And the fourth one came later that night and it is the one that frightened me.
If it is the part of a body that behaves like a thing, then a rule about it is not a rule about a body. It is a rule about property.
Khanom Ansari had said that to me in my first week. She had said: it was not a wall, it was a label. She had said: so a man in the road could tell whose you were.
I had written it down at fourteen and carried it for three years and not understood one word of it.

What came off the nurse in the water, by the way, was nothing of her own. She had never been stopped in her life; she had been out of the country for most of the years when it would have happened. What she was carrying was her sister's, who had not left, and who she will not discuss, and whose hair she does herself at the kitchen table every six weeks because her sister will not come into a shop.
LONG, DYED DARK, ROOTS DONE EVERY SIX WEEKS WITHOUT FAIL.
Shaghayegh came every six weeks on a Tuesday and had done since before I started, and I did her colour, and had done since I was fifteen, which was the first colour my aunt ever let me do on my own.
She was twenty-five. She worked in an office that did something with freight. She had a laugh that made the whole shop turn round.
And her hair was dyed dark, all over, every six weeks, without one single missed appointment in four years. Not a week late. Not once. My aunt used to say she could set the calendar by her.
I did the roots. You do the parting first, then you section, then you work out from the crown. I had my hands on that scalp for forty minutes every six weeks for four years.
And here is the thing that I think about more than almost anything else in this book.
I never once asked what I was covering.
The front of her hairline was white. Not grey — white, and only at the front, in a band about four fingers wide, and underneath and behind it she was dark the way a twenty-five-year-old is dark.

I had known that about her for four years the way you know the pattern on your own kitchen floor. I had mixed the colour for it. I had learned to take it right to the skin at the front because that was the bit that showed first. We had a joke about it. She used to say, mind the stripe. I want it on the record that for four years I thought I was the one making her laugh.
Mind the stripe.

That was the joke, for four years, between a girl of fifteen and a woman of twenty-one who went white at the front in one season at the age of twenty-one, and who came back every six weeks for the rest of her life so that nobody would ask her about it, and who paid me to put the brush right up to the skin.
And nothing ever came off her in the water. Not for four years.

I have thought hard about why and I think I know, and it is not mystical and I am not going to pretend it is. I did not wash Shaghayegh's hair. I coloured it. Colour is dry hair, gloves, a brush, a bowl, a timer. My hands were never in the water on her head, not once in four years, because the rinse at the end is done by whoever is free and it was usually my aunt.
Four years. Six weeks apart. Thirty-four times, or something near it. And the one week in Dey when my aunt had flu and I did the rinse as well as the colour was the week I found out.
THE SAME AS ALWAYS. AND I DID THE RINSE MYSELF.

My aunt had flu in Dey and I ran the shop with a woman she brought in for the week, and on the Tuesday Shaghayegh came for her roots and I did the whole thing, the colour and the timer and then the rinse.
I tipped her back and put my hand under the back of her head to lift it off the porcelain.
Nothing happened to her. They took her sister.

Her sister is three years older. I am not going to write what she was taken for because I do not actually know — I know what came into me and what came into me was not the charge, it was the four years.
Because it was four years.
Shaghayegh was twenty-one. And for four years she did the following things, every week, on top of having a job.

She went to the place you go. She queued. She found out which window, and then the window changed, and she found out again. She learned which days you could bring food and what you were allowed to bring and the exact size the bag had to be. She learned the name of a man who would take the bag in if you were late and what you gave him.
She found the money. All of it. Her family had some and then they did not have some. She sold a gold bangle that was her grandmother's and she did not tell her mother for a year.
She found a lawyer, then a second lawyer, because the first one took the money and did not do anything, which she says happens and which she says you cannot complain about to anybody.

She put up a property. Not hers — there was nothing of hers. She stood in an office and watched her parents sign a paper against the flat they lived in, so that her sister could be out for a certain number of months, and she was the one who had arranged it and she was the one who had to sit in the room while it happened.
And she took the telephone calls. Six in the morning, mostly, because that is when they come. Four years of a telephone going at six in the morning in a flat with four people in it.
And she went every single time. Every visit. Four years.
Her sister served the sentence.
And Shaghayegh served the sentence.

Nobody wrote her name down anywhere in any of it. She has no file. She was not charged with anything and not convicted of anything and not sentenced to anything. If you went to every office in this city and asked what it cost to hold her sister for four years, every single answer you got would be about her sister.

I finished the rinse. I towelled her and sat her up and she looked at me in the mirror and said, mind the stripe, and I said, I know, and she laughed, and I went into the back and put both hands flat on the wall.
WHITE AT THE FRONT ONLY, AND IT CAME IN ONE SEASON.

Here is what Shaghayegh's hair kept, and I did not get this from the water. I got it from the water and then I went and checked it against the thing I already knew about hair, and the two of them fitted, and it is the worst arithmetic in this book.
A third of her hair fell out.
Not all at once in the way people mean when they say that. Over about six weeks. In the shower, on the pillow, in the brush, in handfuls.
And it did not happen when her sister was taken.
It happened three months after.
I need to say why that matters, in the plainest words I have, because when I worked it out I had to sit down on the step in the yard in the cold.

Hair does not come out when the thing happens. It cannot. What happens when something goes through you is that the hair on your head stops growing and sits there. It just stops. And it stays on your head, looking exactly like hair, for about three months. And then it lets go.
So everybody's hair tells you what happened to them three months ago. Everybody's. Yours. Mine.

Which means that for every woman in that book, the worst week of her life and the week her hair came out are two different weeks, and the second one is always the quiet one. The one where it is over. The one where nobody is bringing food any more and nobody is telephoning and everybody has gone back to work and you are supposed to be relieved.
Shaghayegh's hair came out in the week her sister came home.

Four years of queues and bags and six o'clock telephone calls and a bangle and her parents' flat, and she got through all of it with her hair on her head, and then her sister walked in the door, and there was a party, actually, a small one, with the family, and Shaghayegh made the rice.
And three weeks later she was pulling it out of the plughole with a fork.
It came back white at the front. Only at the front, only in that band, and it has stayed white, and she will be white at the front at sixty.
And what her body kept is one thing and it is very small.
She cannot make a telephone call.

She can answer one. She can talk on one for an hour. She cannot place one. She cannot press the numbers and hold it and wait for somebody to pick up. Four years of six in the morning did that, and it did not go away when the four years ended, and it has not gone away since.
So when there is a call to make — the dentist, the office, the man about the boiler — she hands the telephone to her sister, and her sister makes it.
Her sister, who did the four years inside.
Her sister is completely fine on a telephone.
And that is the only place in this entire book where I am going to put down a thing I worked out myself, in my own words, and it is this.
You cannot make a house afraid twice.

They took one woman out of that flat and they got four years of her life. And what they spent to do it was spent on a family where nobody — not the mother, not the father, not Shaghayegh, not her sister — covers anything any more. Not out of politics. They just stopped. It fell off them. They had already had the worst of it and there was nothing left to hold over them, and they knew it, and I think the people who do this know it too and have no way of saying so to each other.
MINE.
I washed my own hair at the basin after we shut, in Esfand, alone, with the shutters down and one light on at the back.
I had been working up to it for a month and I had not admitted to myself that this was what I was doing.

It is not easy to do. The basin is made for somebody else's head. I had to kneel on the floor and get my neck into the dip sideways and run the water with one hand, and I did it properly, both hands in it, the way I do it on a customer, flat palm under the back of the head.
And nothing came.
I did it again two days later, and nothing came.

I did it a third time in Farvardin and knelt there on the wet tiles with the water running over my wrist for much longer than you should, and nothing came, and I sat back against the cupboard with my hair in my face and understood that there was nothing to come.

I had not been stopped except for eight seconds outside a fruit shop with a bag of oranges. I have never been in a van. I have never signed anything. Nobody has ever telephoned my father, who is not in this and never has been. My name is in no office. I have never lost a day's work or a day's school or a single thing I wanted.
My column is empty.

I was seventeen years old and I had two hundred and ninety-odd heads in a book and eighty of them had something in the second column, and I had the only copy, and I was the only person in it who had paid nothing.
I would like to be able to write that I was relieved. I have read that sentence back a number of times and it is the only place in this book where I have tried to make myself sound better than I was.

What I actually felt, kneeling on those tiles, was something I did not have a word for until much later and which I am fairly sure was shame. Not guilt. Guilt is for something you did. I had not done anything. It was the other thing, the one where you look at what you have got and you understand that somebody bought it and that it was not you.
Because here is what I could see, and I could only see it because of the book, which nobody else had.

I walk down a street at seventeen with my scarf halfway back off my head, and when a shopkeeper's son looks at me it is just a boy looking at a girl and not a matter anybody has standing in. And the reason for that is not that the rule changed. The rule did not change. The rule is exactly where it was.

The reason is Khanom Ansari's twenty-two years, and Hengameh's three hours and her thirteen years at a kitchen sink, and the teacher's six years in a room with no window, and Shaghayegh's four years of six o'clock telephone calls, and two hundred-odd more whose names are not in my book because I never wrote the names down.

Every one of them paid on her own. None of them knew any of the others. Nobody thanked a single one of them, and nobody is going to, and there is no office that would even know how to accept the thanks.
And I got the street.
I put the book in my bag and I mopped the floor and I locked the back and I went home and my aunt had left me food.
TO THE SHOULDER. THE PARTING. SHE IS SEVENTY-FOUR.
Khanom Ansari came on the first Saturday of Ordibehesht and I said something to her that I had been carrying for three years.
I said: Khanom Ansari, in my first week you told me about the old law. The one where the wife covered and the woman who was owned was forbidden to.
And she said: did I.
And I said yes. And you said it was not a wall, it was a label.
She did not open her eyes. She said: well. It is.
And I said: I think I have only just understood it.
And she said: go on, then.
So I told her, with my hands in her hair, and it came out badly because I had never said it out loud.
I said: if the covering was to keep women safe from men, then the first woman you would cover is the one with nobody. The one anybody can do anything to. The slave. The one in the street at night.
And instead the law said she was forbidden. On pain of being burned.

So it was never for her. It was never about keeping anybody safe at all. It was a sign you put on a woman so that a stranger could tell what kind she was and whose she was, and that is a thing you do to property, and the only reason it is always hair is that hair is the part of a person that behaves like a thing — you can put a cloth over it, you can take it off, you can measure it.
And then I said the part I had not planned to say.

I said: which is why nobody can answer me. For three years. Not one person. Not because they are lying. Because there is nothing there to say. It is not a reason that came out badly. There was never a reason in it at all. There is only a thing nobody will say.

And Khanom Ansari, who was seventy-four years old and had been sent home at ten in the morning over a piece of cloth and never let back in, lay there with her eyes shut and her neck in the porcelain, and said:
Yes.
That is all she said. Yes. One word, and then she asked whether the water was going cold, which was the thing she always asked and which I understood by then was how she ended a subject.
And I did the second wash and towelled her and walked her up to the chair.
And the thing I had said a hundred times — then it is the men — did not come out of my mouth that day, and I noticed it had not, and it did not come out of my mouth again for a long time afterwards.
Not because it was wrong. It was not wrong. It is still not wrong.

It had just become a very small thing to say about what I was looking at. It was a joke about a man on a bus, and I was holding a bill. It was an argument, and I had been having it for three years with people who were not the ones holding the other end of it, in a room with a painted window, while the actual arrangement sat four thousand years underneath and did not need an argument because it had never had a reason.
CAME IN WITH NOTHING ON HER HEAD.
In Tir of that year a woman walked into the shop with nothing on her head.
I want to put that down slowly because of how long I had been waiting for it without knowing that I was.
She came in off the street at about four in the afternoon. She pushed the door and the bell went and she came in and stood at the counter and asked whether anybody could do her a trim.
And her head was bare. There was no scarf pushed back. There was no scarf round her shoulders. There was no scarf in her hand. I looked at her hands.
She was twenty-two. She had walked from the bus stop on the main road, which is about four hundred metres, past the fruit shop and the pharmacy and the two shops with clipboards and the bakery.
My aunt came out of the back and stopped.
And then she said, of course, sit down, Baran will take you.

Nobody said anything about it. Not one word, from anybody, the whole time she was in that shop. There were four other women in there and all four of them had taken their scarves off at the door the way you do, and not one of them said anything, and the thing in that room for about twenty minutes was so loud I could hear it over the dryer.
I washed her hair and nothing came off her at all. Nothing. Twenty-two years old and never stopped once in her life.
And I asked her — I had to, I was seventeen — I said, you walked here like that?
And she said: from the bus.
And I said: and nobody said anything?
And she said, and I have this exactly, because I wrote it on the loose paper at the back of the book that evening:
Not on our street. Not for a while now. You should try it.
Not on our street. Not for a while now.

She was not being brave. She was not making a point. She did not know she was doing anything at all. She had worked out, from walking about, that on those particular four hundred metres, at that particular time of day, nothing would happen — and she was right, and nothing did.
That is the first entry in my book with nothing in the first column.
Came in with nothing on her head.

And I sat at the till and looked at those words for a while, because the first column was supposed to be a measurement. It was supposed to be the thing you could see from the pavement and the thing the window was painted over for. And here was a head that had already been seen from the pavement, by a hundred people, for four hundred metres, before it ever got to me.
What exactly was I measuring?
I did not understand what was happening to my own book yet. I thought it was one woman.
By the end of that year it was fourteen of them.
TO THE WAIST, AND A MESSAGE CAME TO HER HUSBAND ABOUT
That autumn the second column started to change and I changed with it.

Up until then, everything in it had a place and a person. A van. A door. A courtroom. A room with no window. An office with a clipboard. You could point at the thing that had done it, even if you could not do anything about it.
And then I started getting these.

A woman came in in Aban with hair to her waist and what came off her was a photograph. Not one she had been shown. Not one that was taken by anybody standing in front of her. She had been somewhere — a street, a square, she does not know which — and something had taken her picture, and some days later a message arrived on a telephone.
Not hers. Her husband's.
It had her name in it and the place and the day.

She never saw the photograph. She does not know what she looked like in it. She does not know who has it or where it is or whether it is still anywhere. There is no office she could go to and ask, because asking is the same as telling them you want to know, and she does not know which office to ask anyway.

And what it cost her is not a day or a fine or a year. It is that there is now a thing with her name on it, in a place she cannot locate, which somebody can look at, and she will not find out about it until it is used.
Her hair keeps nothing. There is nothing in it. That is what I had to write and it is why I started writing the second column smaller.
Because this is where the arithmetic I had been doing stopped working.
The van cost them four men's wages and an afternoon, and it bought them four months of Hengameh.
Fifteen years in a courtroom cost them a public record and a number the whole world repeated, and it bought them a nineteen-year-old with her scarf in her bag.

A photograph taken by nobody and a message sent to a husband costs them almost nothing. No wages. No van. Nobody has to stand on a pavement in the cold. One man at a desk somewhere, who has never met her, who presses a thing.
So I thought: that is clever. That is them getting cheaper. That must be better for them.
And it is not. That is the part that took me another year.
Because she was back on the street inside a week. Of course she was. Nothing had happened to her. Nothing had been done to her body. She had not lost a day.
What she had lost was her husband's peace, and he is now the one who checks the telephone.

They have moved it. The whole thing has moved off her and onto him. He is a perfectly ordinary man who sells plumbing fittings and he has not been accused of anything, and he now looks at a screen every evening, and that is where the rule lives in that house now.
I wrote it small. Not to hide it. Because my hand had started doing a thing by then.
CUT TO THE JAW, ALL ONE LENGTH, AS ALWAYS.
My aunt took me to a dentist in Azar because of my jaw.

I had started doing a thing in my sleep, and in the day as well, and I did not know I was doing it. She knew. She had been watching it for a year. She said it in the way she said everything, which was while doing something else.
She said: you are grinding your teeth. There is a man on the main road. We are going on Thursday.

The dentist was about forty and perfectly nice and he looked in my mouth for a while and he said the back two on the left were going flat and he could make me a thing to wear at night and I should try to be less worried about the examination.

That is what he decided it was. The examination. Which was reasonable — I was seventeen and three-quarters, everybody my age was being destroyed by the examination, and he must have had four of us a week. It is the first time in my life I was glad of it. For about a year the examination covered for me the way a cousin covers for you.
In the car afterwards my aunt said: is it the examination.
And I said yes.
And she looked at the road for a while and then she said: all right.

She knew it was not the examination. I know she knew because of the way she said all right — not the way you say it when you believe somebody, the way you say it when you have decided not to make them lie twice.

And I was not going to tell her, for the same reason I had not told her for three years, which is that she had burned eighteen years of names in a barrel in a yard and I had worked out by then that you do not hand a thing like this to a person like that.
So we drove home and she bought me a cake on the corner like I was nine.
That was the same week I noticed what my own handwriting had been doing.
I had gone back through the book looking for something and I got to the pages from about the middle of the second year and I saw it.
The first column is the same all the way through. It firms up over the five years the way anybody's does between fourteen and nineteen, but it is the same hand, the same size, the same slope.
The second column gets smaller.
It starts the same size as the first. By the middle of the second year it is noticeably smaller. By that autumn it is tiny — cramped, down in the corner of the line, in letters about half the height.

And I did not decide to do that. Not once. There was no day where I thought I will write this part smaller. My hand did it on its own over three years, forty seconds at a time, at a till, with a dryer going.
I sat in the shop that night with the book open at two pages, one from the first month and one from that week, and I looked at them side by side.

And the only thing I could think, and I am not going to dress it up, was: so this is what it looks like from the outside. This is what it looks like when it is in a person's hand instead of in her body.

I washed my aunt's hair that evening and nothing came, as it never did, and she cut it herself to the jaw at the mirror, all one length, as she always did, and stood and looked at it for three seconds too long, and said right, and went and put the kettle on.
THREE HUNDRED AND FORTY-ONE HEADS. FOURTEEN OF THEM CAME IN BARE.
On the last night of Esfand I counted it again, the way I had two years before, at the kitchen table with the serial on in the front room.
Three hundred and forty-one heads.
A hundred and nine with something in the second column.
And fourteen that came in off the street with nothing on their heads at all. Fourteen, in one year, where the year before there had been none in four.
I put the three numbers on the loose paper at the back and then I sat there and I finally put the two things together, and it took about a minute, and once it was done it could not be undone.
My mother in the shoe shop: the number did not change. The shoe got worse.
And my book.
Here is what my book says, and it is the only thing in it that nobody told me and nobody could have.
They have never lowered the price.

They are still paying it. A van still costs a van. A court still costs a court. A man at a door still costs a man at a door. Nobody in any office in this country has reduced what they are willing to spend on a woman's head — if anything they have found new ways to spend, the photograph and the message and the thing that sends it.
And what they get for it goes down every single year.
Twenty-two years of Khanom Ansari's life, in exchange for one morning's work by a polite man at a door — and a whole building full of women who did not put a foot wrong for a decade.
A van and an afternoon and four wages — and four months of Hengameh.
Fifteen years, read out in a court, in public, in a number the whole world said out loud — and a nineteen-year-old on a bus saying nobody says anything any more on our street.
A photograph taken by nothing and a message sent to a husband — and she was back out in a week and now he is the one who cannot sleep.
The same money. Less and less in the bag.

And nobody did that to them. Nobody organised it, nobody declared it, there is no committee anywhere that voted for it. They did it to themselves, one woman at a time, for forty years. Nobody in the entire arrangement has ever had to sit in a room and be told that this is what the money was going on. Every single woman they took and did not break made the next woman slightly less afraid, and the two of them never met, and never spoke, and will never know the other one existed, and that is why there is nobody to arrest for it.
That is in a school exercise book with a cardboard cover, in a drawer under a till, in a shop with a painted window, in the handwriting of a girl of eighteen, and it is written nowhere else on earth.

I did not know what to do with it. I want to be honest: I did not think of it as dangerous. I thought of it as mine, which is a stupid thing to think about a book with three hundred other people's lives in it, and which I only stopped thinking in Mehr of the following year, when a man came into the shop with a folder and asked my aunt, very politely, for her appointment books.
IV. THE RECKONING
The man with the folder told me this on his second visit, and he was not trying to help me. It was the material of his job and he was passing the time while my aunt looked for something.
He said: people think we are the only ones.
He said it almost kindly. He had a bad back and he kept shifting in the chair.

He said: we are not the only ones. In the country next door it is the law too, and it is harder than ours. There was an order a few years ago that women should wear the full covering. And here is the part nobody here knows — in their law the punishment does not fall on the woman. It falls on her father, or her nearest male relative. They go to him. He is visited. He can lose his post. He can be put inside.

He said: and then a few years after that they put out a whole law, article by article, and one of the articles says a woman is required to cover her entire body, and that she should cover her face, and — he looked at the ceiling to get it right — and that a woman's voice is also something that should be concealed.
He said: her voice.
Then he said: in one province of a country far away from here, in the east, there is a provincial law, and they have men who patrol for it, and they put the cane on people.
And he said: and in one country in Africa it was the law for thirty years and then it was not.
I said: what happened?
And he said: they stopped describing themselves that way.
Then he looked at his hands and said something that I have turned over ever since, because I do not think he meant anything by it at all.
He said: it is a short list. For something that is supposed to be the natural order of things, it is a very short list.
And I said: it is getting shorter.
And he said yes, without any particular feeling, the way you agree about the weather.
And I said: and nobody who took their name off that list ever stood up and said so, did they.
And he thought about it, properly, for a few seconds, like a man checking a figure.
And then he said: no. I suppose they didn't.

And my aunt came back with the thing he had asked for, and he put his pen on it, and that was the end of the only conversation about any of this that I ever had with anybody from that side of it in my life.
CAME IN WITH NOTHING ON HER HEAD. SO DID THE NEXT ONE. SO DID THE ONE AFTER THAT.
By Farvardin I had stopped being able to use the first column.
It had taken about a year and it had happened without one single announcement, which I had learned by then is how everything in this country happens.

Three in a row, one Tuesday morning. Then four out of six on a Thursday. Then a week where I wrote came in with nothing on her head so many times that I started just writing bare and then stopped writing anything at all, because what exactly was I recording?

The first column was supposed to be the thing you could not see from the street. That was the whole point of it. That was what the paint on the window was for. I had spent four years writing down a private fact, and the private fact had walked out of the shop and onto the pavement and gone to the bakery.
So the first column died.

It did not die because I gave up on it. It died because it was a measurement of a secret and the secret was over. There is a stretch of about thirty pages near the end of that book where the first line is almost nothing — bare, bare, bare, scarf round her shoulders, bare — and the second line goes on and on.
And that is the thing I want somebody to notice if anybody ever reads it.
The street got freer and the bill kept arriving.

Every week, still. A fine. A business. A message to a husband. A nephew. A place at a university. The second column did not slow down at all. If anything there was more in it, because by then they had the cheap methods and the cheap methods can be used on everybody.
So anybody looking at that book from the outside, in one of the two ways people look at this country, would be wrong.
If you only read the first column you would say: look, it is over, they have won, the women are bare-headed on the street, what is everybody complaining about.
And if you only read the second column you would say: nothing has changed at all, it is exactly what it was.

And both of those are in the same book, on the same page, in two lines, in the same handwriting, and they are both true, and I did not do that on purpose. I wrote down what was there, which is the only instruction I was ever given.
BARE. SEVENTEEN. GOOD HAIR, NEVER COLOURED, NEVER CUT SHORTER THAN THIS.

A girl of seventeen came in on a Wednesday in Ordibehesht with her mother, who wanted a colour, and she was seventeen and she sat and waited and then said she might as well have a wash while she was there.
She had come from school. She had her bag. She was bare-headed and so was her mother and neither of them had a scarf anywhere about them that I could see.
I washed her hair and nothing came.

That is not unusual. A hundred and whatever pages of that book say nothing. But I had got to the point where I could tell the difference between a head with nothing in it and a head with nothing in it yet, and this was neither. There was something wrong with it. It was like putting your hand into a drawer you know has a thing in it and finding the drawer empty.

So I did something I had never done. I went back in. I did a second wash she had not asked for, and then at the end I did the rinse myself when I did not need to, which gave me a third go, and I kept my hand flat on the back of her head for longer than you should.
Nothing. Nothing. Nothing.
And then at the chair, while my aunt was doing her mother, she told the whole shop about it herself, in about ninety seconds, laughing, in the voice girls that age use for things that are not funny.
She said: oh, I got stopped in Esfand.
Somebody asked what happened.
She said: nothing happened. They took my name. A woman took a photograph of me on a telephone. I was there about four minutes. Then I got a message and that was that.
And her mother said, from the chair, without turning round: tell her about your father.
And she said: oh. Yeah. They sent one to my dad as well.
And that is the whole of it. Four minutes on a pavement in Esfand, a photograph on a telephone, a message to her, a message to him.
She was back out the next morning with her head bare, and she did not think of herself as having done anything, and she was right, because by then on that street she had not done anything.
I sat at the till with the book open for a long time that afternoon.
Because by then I could do the arithmetic in my head the way you do multiplication, and hers came out at the bottom of it.

Four minutes. One photograph. Two messages. It is the cheapest thing they have ever done to anybody in my book, by a distance, and the whole of what it bought them was one night. She was out again before the shop opened.
The first column of her entry says bare. The second column of her entry says nothing at all.
And it is a lie, and it took me a month to find out why.
HER MOTHER'S. A COLOUR, AND SHE TALKED THE WHOLE TIME, AND I DID THE RINSE.
her mother came back for her roots a month later, and this time I did the rinse, and I found out where her entry had gone.
It had gone to her father.
It is in his house. It is not in her head at all.
Here is what came, and I am going to put it down flat because it is the quietest thing in this book and I think it is the thing I understand least and like least.
He is a man of about fifty. He has a shop that sells fittings for plumbers — brass things, in drawers, with the sizes written on the drawers in marker.
He got a message on a Thursday in Esfand. It had his daughter's name in it and the name of a street and a date.
That is all that has ever happened to him. Nobody has visited him. Nobody has telephoned him. Nothing has been done to his shop. He has not been accused of one single thing.
And he has not spoken a full sentence to his daughter in a year.

He is not angry with her. That is the part his wife said out loud at the mirror, to my aunt, in the ordinary voice you use for a family problem. She said: he is not angry with her. He asks about her at dinner, to me, with her sitting there.
He answers the door himself now. He did not use to. If somebody knocks, he goes.
He looks at his telephone in the evening. Not scrolling — looking. His wife said he picks it up and looks at it and puts it down and does it again twenty minutes later, every evening, for a year.

Because the first message was the first message. And nobody has ever told him whether there is a second one. There is no office he can ring and ask. If he went anywhere and asked, the asking would be the thing that put him on a list, and he is a man who sells brass fittings and he knows that much.

So he waits. He has been waiting for a year. He will probably wait for the rest of his life, and nothing will come, and the waiting is the whole of the punishment, and it has no end date because nobody set one, because nobody is administering it, because there is nobody at the other end of it at all.
Four minutes. One photograph. Two messages.
They have found a way to take a man's evenings for a year and spend nothing.
And his daughter is bare-headed on the street every day and does not know, because nobody has told her, because her mother decided not to and her father cannot form the sentence.
That is in my book under her mother's head, in handwriting about half the height of the line above it, and when I had written it I went out into the yard and stood there for a while in the dark.
MINE. AGAIN. FOURTH TIME.
In Tir I went out to be stopped.

I have never told anybody this and I am aware of how it sounds. I was eighteen and I had just finished the examination and I had three hundred and seventy women in a book in my bag and nothing of my own in any of them.

I did it on a Thursday because Thursdays are busy. I went to the big square at the top of the main road, the one with the metro mouth and the men selling socks, where there used to be a van parked on the corner by the bank, and I know there used to be because Hengameh told me which corner.
And I went with my head bare and my scarf folded in my bag, and I walked up and down that pavement for two hours and forty minutes.
I need to say what I was actually doing, because I have had to be honest with myself about it since.

I was not being brave. I want that struck out before anybody decides it. I was not making a point and there was nobody with me and I did not take a photograph of it and I have never once told it as a story.
I was trying to get a line in my own column.

That is all it was. I was eighteen and I had spent four years writing down what other women had paid, and I had worked out that I had paid nothing, and I could not stand it, and I went out to buy something so that I would be in the book I was keeping.
And nothing happened.

Nobody said anything to me. There was no van on that corner and I do not think there had been one for a long time. A woman at a bus stop with grey hair looked at my head for about two seconds and then looked away and I could not tell you what she was thinking and I have thought about her ever since.
A man selling socks called me sister and asked if I wanted socks. He called every woman on that pavement sister for two hours and forty minutes and I was the only one of us conducting an experiment.
At one point a police car went past and I stood still like an idiot and it went past.

And at about half past six I sat down on the step outside a sandwich place and understood what I had actually done, which is that I had gone out and tried to pay a debt at a counter that had been closed.
Because that is what it is. It is closed.
Not forgiven. Nobody forgave anybody. Not changed — the rule is exactly where it was, word for word, and the man with the folder came into our shop about eight weeks later with that rule in his hand.

Not announced, either. Nobody stood up anywhere and said, we have stopped collecting on that street at that hour. There is no such day. Khanom Ansari spent her whole life looking for the day they started and I have spent four years looking for the day they stopped and neither of those days exists.

The window is just shut. There is nobody behind it. And it can open again tomorrow and nobody will announce that either, and when it does, every woman in my book will have paid for a street that somebody else will have to buy back.
I walked home with my scarf still in my bag. My aunt was asleep in the chair with the serial on.
I wrote mine, again, fourth time, still nothing at the kitchen table and then I sat there for a while.

I had gone out at eighteen years old with my head bare to buy a line in a ledger. I am aware that there are women in that book who would have given a great deal to be as bored as I was that afternoon. I do not know whether what I did was the most selfish thing in the book or the only honest thing in it, and I have had a year and I still do not know.
NOT A HEAD. A MAN CAME IN.
He came in on a Tuesday in Shahrivar at about half past four.
The bell went and I thought it was a customer and I came out of the back with wet hands.

He was about forty-five. A grey jacket, no tie. A cardboard folder under his arm with an elastic band round it, the kind that has a flap. He was not big and he was not frightening and he had a bad back, which I could see immediately because of the way he stood with one hand at the base of his spine.
There were two women in the shop with their heads uncovered. They put their scarves on. Nobody said anything. One of them did it so fast she pulled her own hair.
He said good afternoon and he asked for the person responsible for the premises.
My aunt came out. She had gloves on with colour on them. She took them off very slowly and put them in the bin and wiped her hands on a towel and said, that is me.
And then she said: sit down, you look like your back is hurting.
And he said, thank you, and sat down in the second chair, in a women's salon, with two customers in scarves pretending to read, and he put the folder on his knees.

He was polite the entire time. I want that understood, because it is the whole of what I have to say about him. He did not raise his voice. He did not threaten anybody with anything. He said Khanom every time he addressed her, and when my aunt offered him tea he said that was very kind of her and he would not, and he looked as though he meant it.
He was so polite that after about four minutes I began to feel that I had done something to him.
He said he was from a provincial office and he named it and I am not going to write the name because I never wrote any names.
He said he was doing a routine review of licensed premises in the district.
He asked how long she had held the licence. She told him. He wrote it down.
He asked whether the window treatment was in compliance. She said he was welcome to look. He looked, from inside, standing on nothing, from about a metre away, and said that it appeared satisfactory.
He asked about the hours. He asked whether any men were employed on the premises. He asked whether any events were held after hours.
And then he said: and you keep an appointment book.
And my aunt said: yes.
And he said: I would like to see the last three years of it.
And she said: I keep one year.
And he said: one year?
And she said: one year. Then I throw it away. I have the current one and the one before it. The rest go.
And he looked at her for a moment and wrote something down, and said: is that your practice.
And she said: that is my practice.

It was not. It had been eighteen years in a stack in that drawer and she had burned every single one of them in a barrel in the yard on a Thursday night four and a half years earlier, and the only person on earth who knew that was standing six feet away with wet hands.
He said he would like to collect the two books on Mehr the second, and he would appreciate it if they were ready.
And she said they would be ready.

And he thanked her, and he stood up with his hand at his back, and he said the thing I have never been able to get out of my head, which he said at the door, kindly, as a sort of apology for the inconvenience.
He said: it is nothing to do with you, Khanom. We are only trying to establish how it started.
NOBODY. WE DID NOT OPEN.
On the twenty-fifth of Shahrivar a woman died in custody and this country came apart.
I am not going to write her name here.

I want to say why, because it is not squeamishness and it is not fear. It is that there are no names in my book. Not one, in five years, in three hundred and seventy-odd entries. My aunt burned eighteen years of names in a barrel and handed me a blank exercise book the next morning, and whatever she meant by it, what I built out of it was a record with no names in it at all.
And her name is in every mouth in this country and it will be in every mouth in this country for a hundred years. It does not need my book. My book is for the ones whose names are nowhere.
The shop did not open for a week.

I was eighteen. I will not describe that week, partly because everybody who was here has their own and does not need mine, and partly because I was not in it. I was in a flat with my aunt, who would not let me out of the door, and who did not sleep, and who sat up with the television on with the sound down the way she had in Aban two years before.
And on the fourth night of it she said something to me in the kitchen at about two in the morning, with her back to me, filling the kettle she had already filled.
She said: Baran. Where is the book.
And I said: in my bag.
And she said: not in the shop?
And I said no. I take it home every night.
And she stood there with the tap running into a full kettle for about four seconds.
And then she said: good.
And then she said: do not bring it into the shop again.
And I said, Khaleh, I have to write in it, I write in it at the till —
And she turned round and said: write it on something else and put it in the book at home.
And I said all right.
And she said: and if anybody asks you what you write at the till, it is the stock.
And I said all right.
And she said: say it.
And I said: it's the stock.

She nodded and turned the tap off and poured the whole kettle away and filled it again, and we did not say another word about it, and I did exactly what she told me for the next three weeks, which is why there is a loose piece of paper folded into the back of that book with nine entries on it in pencil that I never copied over.
There is a page in my book for that week and the first line says nobody, we did not open and the second line has a dash on it.

A dash. I could not write anything. Three hundred and seventy women, every single one of whose prices I had put down in that column for five years, and for that week I sat with the book open on the kitchen table and could not think of one unit that it went in.
BARE. BARE. BARE. ALL OF THEM. SEVEN BEFORE NOON.
We opened again and the shop was full and every head in it was bare.
Not some of them. All of them.

They did not come in and take their scarves off at the door. They came in off the pavement with nothing on their heads, one after another, all morning, and sat down and talked about ordinary things, and the painted window was still painted and the licence was still in the frame and a man was coming on the second of Mehr for the books.
My aunt did not say anything about it. She did the work. At about noon she went into the back and stayed there for a bit and came out again.
The man came on the second of Mehr at ten in the morning, exactly as he had said.
My aunt had the two appointment books on the counter with an elastic band round them.

He sat in the second chair again with his hand at his back and went through them. It took about twenty minutes. He had a pencil and he made a mark in his own folder every so often, and once he turned a book round and asked her what a word was, and she told him, and it was a woman's surname written badly.
And while he did it, with nothing else to do, he talked.

That is when he told me about the other countries. I have put the whole of it at the front of this part, because it does not belong in a morning with two appointment books on a counter and a woman under a dryer.

What belongs here is the end of it. He said it was a short list. For something that is supposed to be the natural order of things, a very short list. And he agreed, without any particular feeling, the way you agree about the weather, that it was getting shorter — and that nobody who had come off it had ever stood up and said so.
Then he shut the second book and put his hands flat on it and said:
Khanom, forgive me. These are appointments.
And my aunt said: yes.
He said: names, days, times.
She said: yes.
And he said: I am not looking for who came to the shop. I can see who came to the shop. I am trying to establish who began it.
And my aunt said: began what?
And he said — and this is exactly what he said, and I had my hand on the edge of the counter — he said:
This. On this street. Somebody must have been first.
And there was a silence of about three seconds, and then my aunt said, in the most ordinary voice in the world, the voice she used for the price of chicken:
I have been on this street for twenty-two years. Nobody was first.
And he said: somebody is always first, Khanom.
And she said: not with this.

He wrote something down. I do not know what. Then he put the elastic band round the two books and handed them back to her, which I had not expected, and said that he would be in touch if anything further was required, and he thanked her for her time, and at the door he said it was nothing to do with her, which was the second time he had said it, and I believe he believed it both times.
And then he was gone, and the bell went, and a woman under the dryer said, what did he want?
And my aunt said: nothing. He wants to know who started it.
And a woman in the end chair, who was about sixty and who had sat there all the way through it with a bare head and a magazine, said:
Started what? I'm sixty-one years old. I'm just hot.
And the whole shop went. Properly went. My aunt laughed until she had to sit down on the arm of the chair, which I had seen her do perhaps four times in five years.
That is the best thing anybody said in that shop in five years and I did not say it.

And I stood at the back with my hands in a towel and did not laugh, because I had just watched a man spend three weeks and two visits looking for a name, and I had the only book in that district with the answer in it, and the answer is that there is no name, and I was the only person in the room who could prove it.
HERS. CUT TO THE JAW, ALL ONE LENGTH, AS IT HAS BEEN FOR FIVE YEARS.
Four days later, on the Saturday, after we had shut, my aunt sat down in the chair at the first basin and said: wash my hair.
I had washed her hair perhaps a hundred and twenty times in five years. Every second week. It was a thing we did at the end of a Saturday with the shutters down, the way you do the floor.

She had never asked for it. Not once. She would just be in the chair when I came through from the back, and I would do it, and neither of us would say anything about it, and nothing would come, and I would write nothing on the second line and that would be that.
This time she asked. She said the words. And she sat down in the first chair and not the second, which she never used, and she put her head back and shut her eyes before I had the towel on her.
And I knew. Not the thing — I did not know the thing yet. I knew that she had decided something and that she had picked the chair to do it in.
I want to put down what I understood later about why.
She did not know how it worked. I am certain of that. She never knew, and she never asked, and nobody in this whole book ever explained one single thing about it to me, including me.

But she had watched me for five years. She had watched a girl of fourteen turn into a girl of nineteen at that basin. She had seen me come out of the back room grey. She had taken me to a dentist about my jaw and listened to me say it was the examination and said all right in the voice you use when you have decided not to make somebody lie twice. She had told me, in the second year, out of nowhere, that I did not have to put everything in there. She had said, on a pavement with a cigarette, I do not want you to do it, I want it done.

She had worked out that I knew things. She did not know how and she did not care how. And she had waited five years, and a man had come into her shop twice with a folder looking for a name, and she had sat in a chair with her eyes shut and said wash my hair.
So I washed my aunt's hair.
I turned the water on and ran it over my wrist and it was right. I put the towel across her shoulders. I asked, is it good, and she said yes.
And I put my hand flat under the back of her head and lifted it off the porcelain.
She had a daughter.

I knew that. Everybody knew that. There is a name in our family that is said about twice a year, carefully, at the edge of other sentences. Parisa. I have known that name since I was four years old. I knew there had been a cousin and that she had died a long time before and that you did not ask, the same way you do not ask about anything else in a family, and by nineteen I had stopped even noticing that I had never been told how.

I was six when it happened. I do not remember it at all. There is no memory there to go looking in. There was a photograph on the shelf in the front room at some point and then there was not, and I cannot tell you what year it came down, because that is how those things work: nothing is announced.
She was twenty-one.
And then the rest of it came in, and I stood in my aunt's shop with my hand under her head and the water running and I did not say one word.
TO THE JAW. ALL ONE LENGTH. EVERY SIX WEEKS FOR
FOURTEEN YEARS.
Here is what happened, in the order it came.
Parisa was twenty-one. She was out in the summer in the year I was six, in a month I will not write down because it does not need me to write it down, and she did not come back.
They had her for nine days before they would say so.
And when they would say so, there was a thing that had to be signed before they would let my aunt have her.
It said something about how she died that was not what happened.

My aunt signed it. She signed it in an office, on a Tuesday morning, sitting down, with a pen somebody handed her, and a man watching, and she read it first, and she knew exactly what it said, and she signed it.
And then there was a second part, which I did not know was a thing that happened to people until it came into me off my own aunt's scalp.
The same words had to go on the stone.

Not a note in a file. Not a form in a drawer. The sentence that is not true is cut into the stone over my cousin, in a cemetery I have been to twice in my life, and it is there now, and it will be there in a hundred years, and anybody who walks past it will read it and believe it, because why would they not.
My aunt chose the stone. She chose the lettering. She paid for it.
And it says the thing she was made to sign.
And the reason she signed it — this came in with everything else, in that flat way, like a telephone number — is that it was the ninth day and she wanted her daughter.
That is the whole of it. There was no other reason. A woman signed a lie about her own child's death because she had been standing in corridors for nine days and she wanted to take her home.
I had my hand under her head. The water was running over my wrist. She had her eyes shut and her breathing had not changed.
And then the last two things came, and they are the ones I have not been able to put down for a year.
Her hair.

Parisa wore it to the jaw. All one length. There is a photograph of her like that; it is the one that used to be on the shelf, and I have seen it, and I did not remember it until that minute at the basin, and then I remembered it completely.
My aunt wore hers long. Down her back, in a plait at work. I have seen pictures of that too and never once thought about it.

And on the night they welded the caps onto the boxes so that no woman could stand on one — the night I came down into the yard because I could smell it, and she was feeding eighteen years of appointment books into a barrel with a stick, and I said Khaleh what are you doing and she said go up — on that night, afterwards, she went into the bathroom and cut her own hair to the jaw with the kitchen scissors, badly, and would not let anybody fix it.
I wrote that in my book at fourteen. It is in there, in my first month, in a child's handwriting. Cut to the jaw that morning, by herself, badly.
I thought she was upset about the news.

Those appointment books had my cousin's name in them. Eighteen years of Tuesdays. A girl came to her mother's shop and had her hair done, dozens of times, and her mother wrote her name and the day and the hour in a book with a ring binding, in her own handwriting, because the licence requires it.

And on a Thursday night in Bahman, because a woman had stood on a box and been taken away and the city had welded the boxes shut, my aunt became frightened enough to burn the only record of her daughter's life that existed in this world.
And then she went upstairs and cut her hair to her daughter's length.
She made her own head into the record, because she had just destroyed the paper one.

And she has cut it to that exact length every six weeks since. Fourteen years, counting from the stone. Five of them in front of me. I have watched her do it at that mirror perhaps forty times and stand afterwards with her head a little on one side, looking at it for three seconds longer than a person looks at a haircut, and then say right, and go and put the kettle on.
I thought she was particular about it. I used to be irritated when she would not let me try anything with the front.
And the last thing.
She cannot be in that shop on her own.

Not frightened of anybody. Not of the street, not of men, not of the office with the folder. She simply cannot be in that room alone with the shutters down, and she has not been able to for fourteen years, and she has never said one word about it to anybody alive.
Which is why, when her sister went onto nights at the plant, my aunt was the one who asked for me.

I had believed my whole adolescence that I had been sent to her. I had told people that. My mother went onto nights, the journey was too long, I went to my aunt's — I have said that sentence a hundred times, including in the first page of this book.
She asked for me.

I have been in that shop for five years as a person for a woman not to be alone with, and nobody ever told me, and she fed me, and taught me a trade, and took me to a dentist, and bought me a cake on a corner like I was nine, and never once said why.
I finished washing her hair.
I did the second wash. I towelled it. I asked, is it still good, and she said yes.
And then she opened her eyes and looked at me in the glass and said one word.
She said: Well?
And I said: I know.
And she said: good.

And neither of us said one further thing about it, that night or ever, and she cut her own hair to the jaw at the mirror six weeks later, all one length, and stood and looked at it, and said right, and went and put the kettle on.
THREE HUNDRED AND SEVENTY-FOUR.
He came back on a Thursday in the middle of Mehr. Nobody had telephoned. The bell went just before ten and it was him with the folder under his arm and his hand at the base of his back.
My aunt was not there. She had gone to the wholesaler on the main road for colour and she was forty minutes away at best.
There were three women in the shop, all bare-headed, and they put their scarves on, and one of them put it on wrong and left it.

He said good morning and he asked for the person responsible for the premises and I said she was out and he said he would wait, if that was all right, and I said of course, and he sat down in the second chair.
And then he said: it is you who writes at the counter.
I said yes.
He said: the stock?
And I said: the stock.
And he said: hm.
And then he said, not unkindly, looking at his folder and not at me: how old are you?
I said nineteen.
He said: and you have been here how long?
I said five years.
And he nodded, and he said — and I am putting this down exactly because it is the last thing anybody in authority has ever said to me:
He said: then you have seen the whole of it, haven't you.
And I said yes.
And he said: so you tell me, then. Who was first?
And I want to describe what happened in me, because it took about two seconds and it has governed the rest of my life.

I thought: he is not lying. He genuinely wants a name.
