He has been given a number by somebody above him that he cannot account for, and he has spent weeks on this street going into shops with a bad back, and he has read two years of a hairdresser's appointments, and he is sitting in a chair in a women's salon on a Thursday morning asking a girl of nineteen for a name, because in his entire training and in his entire office and on every form he has ever filled in, a thing has a cause and a cause has a name.
And he is not going to get one. Not from me, not from anybody, not ever, because it does not exist.
And then I thought about my book.

Three hundred and seventy-four heads. A hundred and thirty-one with something in the second column. Not one name in any of it. Not one line connecting any two women in it. Khanom Ansari did not know Hengameh. Hengameh did not know the teacher. Shaghayegh had sat in a chair next to at least four of the others and talked to them about rice.

And every single one of them paid alone, and nobody thanked one of them, and nobody will, and there is no office anywhere whose job it is to add up the second column, because the cases sit in different courts and different provinces under different articles — a fine here, a suspended sentence there, an administrative matter, an expulsion, a message to a husband's telephone — and the only reason no number exists is that no building was ever built to hold one.
And I had it. In a bag, on a hook, four feet behind him.
So I went and got it.

I went into the back and took it out of my bag and stood with it in my hands for a moment, and then I opened it at the front, at the first page, where I had written my own name at fourteen in the top corner the way children label a schoolbook, with the year next to it in a loopy hand.
And underneath my name, because I had ruled the columns on every page including that one, there was a line, and the first column was empty and the second column was empty.
I tore that page out. One page. I folded it twice and put it in the pocket of my tunic.

Not because I was frightened. I have been through this every day since and I am not going to make it prettier than it is. There were two reasons and they are both true and they do not sit well together.

The first is that the book has no names in it. That is what it is. My aunt burned a book full of names and gave me a blank one the next morning, and whatever she meant by it, a record with no names in it was the thing I built, and my own name on the front page was the only thing in five years that broke it. Taking it out made the book honest.
And the second is that I have paid nothing, and I was not going to be bound in with them.
Then I came out and I gave it to him.
I put it on his knees on top of his folder and I said: this is what we have got.
And he opened it.
And I stood there and watched a man in a grey jacket read the first page, and then turn it, and then turn it, and then stop turning and go back, and read one line twice.
And he did not say anything for a long time.
Then he said: there are no names in this.
And I said: no.
And he said: what is the second line?
And I said: what it cost her.

He looked at it for a while longer. He got to the end — it does not take long, it is four hundred lines — and then he went back to the middle and read two pages properly, which I could tell because of how long it took him.
And then he closed it and sat with both hands flat on the cover, and he said, in a completely different voice from the one he had used about the window and the hours:
What am I supposed to do with this?
And I said: I don't know.
And he said: there is no name in it.
And I said: there isn't one.
And he said — and this is the end of it, this is the whole of what happened, there was no argument and nobody raised their voice and nothing was settled —
He said: then there is nothing for me to write.
And I said: no.
And he sat there with his hands on it for a bit. One of the women under the dryer turned a page of her magazine. Out on the street somebody was backing a van and the beeper was going.
And then he put the book inside his folder and did the elastic band round it, and he stood up with his hand at his back, and he said: I will need to take this.
And I said: I know.
And he said thank you, which I have thought about ever since, and he went out, and the bell went, and I heard him cough once on the pavement.
My aunt came back twenty minutes later with four boxes of colour and said the man had put the price up again.
I said: he took the book.
And she put the boxes on the counter and straightened them, and said: did he say anything?
And I said: he said thank you.
And she looked at the boxes for a bit and then she said: well. They are always very polite when there is nothing in it for them.
And then she asked me to put the kettle on, and I did, and we did four heads that afternoon, and I wrote them on a piece of paper at the till because there was no longer a book to write them in.
I have the page. It is folded twice and it is in a tin with a hinge that was my grandmother's, and it has my name on it, and a year, and two empty columns.

GLOSSARY

chador [chaa-DOR] — a single large piece of cloth, usually black, held closed at the front and covering the body from the head down. Worn over other clothes, and worn by choice by some women and as a uniform by others.
Khaleh [khaa-LEH] — mother's sister. A maternal aunt is called khaleh, on its own or followed by her name. A father's sister is a different word.
Khanom [KHAA-nom] — madam; the ordinary respectful form of address to a woman, used with her family name or on its own. A girl of fourteen would call every customer this.
Nowruz [no-ROOZ] — the new year, at the spring equinox. The weeks before it are the busiest of the year in a hair salon, because everybody wants to be new for it.
Ramadan [ra-ma-DAAN] — the month of fasting.
